sections.content:
Too fundamental. Can be totally replaced by ELEC2400

Course Description

ELEC1100 is designed to provide the fundamental knowledge in electrical engineering, basic electronic components and skills needed for the design, implementation and evaluation of a robot and its subsystems.
It covers the basic electronic engineering principle and techniques.
Hands-on laboratory sessions, complemented with lectures and tutorials, are provided to allow students to have a systematic view of the electronic engineering principles.
Students apply the knowledge and principles learnt to design and build a functional robot by themselves.

Basic concepts like Ohm's law, KCL KVL, diodes, zener diode, transistors, H-bridge, sensors, boolean algebra, Arduino coding

Personally don't like introductory course like this. One bad thing is that because instructors think they are so basic, they won't teach in deep of those concepts but they will test you in deep during written exam. They are easy to learn but difficult to master. During exam I still cannot understand and classify knowledge between diode and zener diode.

But in ELEC2400 will be introduced much deeper but same contents, so I think this course can be replaced by ELEC2400 and other circuit courses.
sections.teaching:
Teaching is okay. Professor Yang can make his effort to explain the ideas in details. Teaching is clear as all.

The IA Tang Yimeng is very good, she is responsible and helpful, once she spent a huge effort and time to help me solving a difficult boolean algebra question.

❖ LAB: 6 lab assignments (30% total).
❖ QUIZ: Pop-up in-class quizzes (open book, 10% total), online submission in iPRS
(20 questions in total, only the top 60% answers will be counted).
❖ EXAM: Lab Exam (close book, 15%) and Written Exam (close book, 20%).
❖ PROJECT: Project demo (20%) and report (5%).

Because this course, most of things are not difficult at all, for example Ohm's law and KCL KVL which we learnt them from DSE physics or PHYS1114.
Many students can basically know everything and get full scores. Making this course very competitive and "bad" grades are determined by how many scores that students lose.

Also beware there are lot of accidents during final project.
1. Mind of the mat, the final demo they will clean the map so the friction will be reduced, and during testing the maps will be probably stepped by others, causing higher friction.
2. Beware of your abnormal teammate. Beware not to get labs score deduction because of them (Of course also make sure that you are also trustworthy). I heard some of my friends encountered uncapable/freerider and really fried the project, getting 10+ overall score deduction.

Any accident will make you in disadvantage in this course, given that grade boundaries are very high.

I know in recent years the project/lab exam difficulties are slightly increased, it reduced the grade cutoffs but cannot reduced the high statistics of this courses.

sections.content:
The course covers a range of fundamental electronic components, from diodes to transistors, along with essential circuit analysis techniques such as Kirchhoff’s Current Law (KCL) and Kirchhoff’s Voltage Law (KVL). Topics also include H-bridge circuits, resistors, and an introduction to basic integrated circuits. In the later stages, the curriculum shifts to hands-on microcontroller programming with the Arduino platform and foundational C++.

The course culminates in a final project: building a line-following robot car. The vehicle is designed to track a white line on a black mat, with an Arduino Nano board serving as its main control unit.

Written Exam 20% (around November)

sections.content: The course material is well-structured, clear, and easy to follow. The tutorials are especially helpful as they include live demos highlighting crucial key takeaways and common pitfalls, making complex concepts much easier to grasp.
sections.teaching: The instructional team is excellent. Special thanks to Tang Yimeng, who is remarkably patient and approachable. Their constructive feedback and insightful guidance were exceptionally beneficial when our team was navigating challenges during the final project.
sections.grading: While the course overall is great, the grading scheme has significant room for improvement. The midterm lab exam carries a high weight of 20%—the exact same percentage as the entire car project！！！—despite consisting of only three questions. This creates high variance and leaves too much to chance！！Unfortunately, a minor misstep on the exam severely damaged my overall grade, keeping me out of the A-range despite achieving top-tier performance on the final project。
sections.workload: The workload is quite heavy, particularly due to the final line-following car project. The timeline is tight, and getting the car to run smoothly requires endless testing, hardware tweaking, and code debugging. While building the car is a rewarding hands-on experience, the time commitment required is considerably higher than what the current grade breakdown suggests.

sections.workload:
前期十分轻松，但这些轻松都是为了铺垫搞final project那时候的高压。
Final Project期间，你会拿到小车和地图，然后你就要根据你小车上的sensor做编程巡线，完成一些动作，走到终点，一个星期后的early demo里，如果你走完全图，那你就可以解放不用再做了；如果你直走到一半，那你有一半的分数加bonus分，剩下那一半可以留到第二个星期跑。你听着很简单，但是实际上你要疯狂测试小车的速度、sensor的灵敏度，甚至是电池的电量。那两个礼拜我其他课程都荒废了，每天一下课都去宿舍搞这个小车，写编程跑小车。
说到宿舍，小车的地图超级无敌大，我的车和地图都是要寄存在别人宿舍的（因为我和队友都没宿舍），我不敢想象没宿舍又没朋友帮忙寄存的人是怎么处理这个问题的。

Final Project焚决：
1.有人把6个sensor都装上车上面然后想几百个情况，一个星期就搞定Project demo。

2.sensor宽度不要一成不变，面对90度弯，如果你只有两个sensor探测地下的白线的话，你可以把sensor距离拉宽一点，这样可以有效减少探测器探测到双白的几率

3.连续90度弯的编程思路，我的思路是算时间，在某个时间区间内如果sensor探测到双白（两个sensor都探测到白色），就执行左/右转90度，counter + 1；如果过了那个时间区间，这代表车子很幸运地通过了90度弯且没探测到双白，counter +1。希望后世看到这个思路能拯救一下他们Project中的瓶颈。

报课焚决：
ECE学生的study pattern里面说建议ECE学生在Year 1 的 Fall term选，所以我猜如果在spring term选的话就不用和ECE学生正面竞争了，但你要面对的是CPEG的学生。
还有个数据：jupas ece学生第一年学额为70个，cpeg学生学额为91个。那个sem报自己决定

那两个星期的折磨我毕生难忘，所以workload给到拉完了

sections.content: This course covers the fundamental knowledge on the design, implementation and evaluation of a robot and its sub-systems. It starts with easy secondary school physics and some important components in a circuit. Overall, you will learn how to design and build a functional robot from scratch. Quite easy to handle.
sections.teaching: Teaching part is okay. I nearly skip all lectures but I can tell it is good and fun. Maybe a little boring. TA is very helpful and nice.
sections.grading: Well, what can I say? Your grade basically depends on luck and your groupmates. Your car project can easily fail even after you've tested it a thousand times.
sections.workload: Relatively low workload. No assignment after lectures. The only thing you need to work on is that stupid project and a 1200 words report for only 3% of the overall scores. All labs are easy. No attendance for lectures.

sections.content:
课程内容跨度很大，从最基础的电路物理知识（Ohm‘s Law， KCL/KVL）一直延伸到数字逻辑电路（Logic Gates， K-map），甚至涉及了简单的微控制器（MCU/Arduino）编程。

前半个学期偏向“复古”，主要手算电阻、电压、二极管电路，虽然略显枯燥且像高中物理的延伸，但这是打地基的关键。到了后半段，课程开始变得炫酷起来，引入传感器、PWM波（脉宽调制）和 H-bridge 电路，所有内容都指向同一个最终目标——做一辆会自动跑的小车。这种“Contextual Learning”（联系上下文/项目导向的学习）设计得很巧妙，让你明白学这些看似过时的电路知识到底有什么用。

美中不足的是，理论课的内容有时候略显松散，部分课可能需要很强的自学能力来补充。
sections.teaching: 这门课的灵魂在实验室。TA 们虽然有时候很忙，但关键时刻能救命。Lab 是这门课的核心，前面的几次实验（KCL， Transistor， H-bridge）都是为 final project 做的铺垫。如果你前几次 lab 是混过去的，final project 大概率会做不出来。ta们超级好！！
sections.grading: 高中知识够拿a
sections.workload:
一个字：肝。
虽然只有4个学分，但实际占用的时间可能是 6 个学分的感觉。

常规周： 听课 + 写 lab report （实验报告通常需要花不少时间整理数据）。

期末周 （Project Week）： 这是真正的考验。你大概率会把人生中第一次“刷夜”献给 ELEC 1100。搭建小车电路板、调试传感器、写 Arduino 代码，你会发现硬件 debug 比软件 debug 玄学得多（“明明是刚接好的线，怎么动了一下就不亮了？”）。

建议：
千万不要拖延！ Final demo 前几天实验室会挤满人，排队等 TA 检查可能要等一小时，万一元件烧了都没地方哭。能早点去实验室就早点去，Early Demo 通常会有额外的加分机会。

sections.content:
The course provides an overview of physics, covering the application and understanding of many physical principles.

Most of the lab work involves building various circuits on breadboards, ranging from simple to complex. Don't worry, TA will help you complete the experiments. Note that there's a time limit for earning bonus points; you must complete the experiments before that time.

The final lesson includes a project on a small robot car that can move along a white line on a map. This requires teamwork; if you encounter any problems during the project, be sure to contact Yimeng for help with debugging.

Most of the lecture content is not difficult and connects to high school physics concepts. The small amount of coding content is also relatively easy to understand if you have a programming background.
sections.teaching: I didn't attend many lectures mostly self- studying.
sections.grading: The robot car project and lab checkpoints carry many weight in final grade, and everyone's grades are very close. Every point is crucial to getting a good grade.
sections.workload: Not too much, but the last two weeks will require more time for the robot car project. Otherwise, you only need to complete the lab assignments; there are no other homework assignments.

sections.content:
The course introduces the fundamental knowledge on the design, implementation and evaluation of a robot and its sub-systems. It covers the basic principles of analog and digital circuits as well as robot sensing and control mechanisms. Students have to apply the knowledge and principles learned to design and build a functional robot by the end of the course. Students who have completed ELEC 2200, ELEC 2350, ELEC 2400, ELEC 2420, or ELEC 3310, must obtain instructor's approval to take this course.
INTENDED
LEARNING
OUTCOMES On successful completion of the course, students will be able to:
1. Recognize the history and development of major ECE fields.
2. Apply the fundamental circuit concepts to compute the output of basic electronic circuits.
3. Analyze, design, and debug simple analog circuits, and design and program for simple digital control strategies.
4. Build a real engineering system following a hierarchical design principle.
5. Work in a team environment, learn and practice effective project management.
6. Execute a complete project from problem formulation, design/implementation, up to verification and documentation.

sections.content:
Covers the very basics of circuit theory, and a basic introduction of designing physical systems.
Circuit theory covered:
- V=IR
- resistors
- KCL and KVL
- regular and zener diodes
- bipolar junction transistors (BJT)
You are also tasked to build a line following robot across all the labs, which are separated by steps for each lab session. A final project demo is used to test the competency of the robot.
sections.teaching: The lectures are not particularly engaging if you are not interested in the topic itself, but very interesting if you are. Professor will stay behind after most classes to answer questions, and can explain in mandarin of needed. Tutorial sessions are held by an assistant and also serve to prepare you for lab sessions.
sections.grading:
First 5 labs 5% each, final lab 4%, 29% lab total
Pop quiz (open book), 3% total, iprs, 6 for full mark, 8 questions
Lab exam 20%
Written exam 25%
Project demo 20%, report 3%

The labs are free points if you work efficiently. There are bonus credits (1 each) for finishing in 1.5 hours. Do not skimp on preparation beforehand and chances are you will be able to score the bonus credits.

I cannot attest to the pop quizzes as I missed all of them.

The lab exam is trivially easy if you study even a little bit. Important things to remember is how to read the polarity of a zener diode (lost >7/20 marks due to this). Forgetting one piece of basic information will get you heavily punished due to the small number of questions.

The written exam is very crammable, but not a good idea. Primarily focused on diode and BJT based circuits, no dynamics at all.

The project demo is very easy if you space out your work over the time given. 2 marks are given if the code compiles and the motors stop spinning after reset. Hard coding the movement is theoretically possible but due to the nature of the components unreliable and shouldn't be relied on. A few marks are given for every few junctions, and a few other additional tasks that your robot must preform.
sections.workload:
Main component of the workload is in the lab projects. If you are new to line following bots, it can be quite a lot to learn. You are given step by step instructions to assemble your robot and to verify it works. Additionally, you are given around a month to fine tune it and program it yourself.

I had prior experience in linebots, so I cannot accurately report on how it is to learn from scratch. However, I managed to finish all the programming in 1 day (do not recommend).

There are no other assignments outside of class for this course.

sections.content:
ELEC 1100 is a very introductory level course covering components and other parts all leading up to the final project which consists of creating a self driving robot that completes a pre asigned path.

Overall the content is very simple and does not take much time to learn and understand.

The course includes the following:
- 17 Lectures
- 3 in tutorial quizzes (worth a percentage of your grade)
- 6 Labs that gear you towards completing your final project
- 1 mid term
- 1 final paper
- 1 final project

The quizzes and labs are very simple and you ca very easily attain full mark

Mid terms consists of a practical paper where you will be tasked with creating circuits in person and using said circuits to find certian voltage or resistance or other values.

I would recommend starting the final project as soon as possible as you will require a good amount of time for it and finshing it fast (by the early demonstration) will give you extra time for your other papers.
sections.teaching:
Lectures will give you a very brief understanding of the parts of the course however do not really show you what the papers will be like at the end of the course.

Tutorials are worth going to as they practically explain how to the upcomming lab and will help you get full marks easily. Additionally, the tutorials will have 3 random (very short, very easy) quizzes which are part of the final percentage of the course.
sections.grading:
Grading in this course is horrible. Try not to lose any percentage points where you can. Attend all tutorials and try to get full marks in the things you can control like the project and the labs.

Personally, i only droppped marks in the final and midterm papers and ended up getting 90+% in this course which lead to only a B+.
sections.workload: Not much workload at all, the only part of the course that gets heavy is the final project. However if you spend a good few hours on the project you will find it fun and intresting especially if your predefined route is not too hard.

sections.content: The content is quite interesting, while the difficulty is managable. Lectures are mainly about the basic formulas and what to do in the labs, and Tutorials are just revisions for the lectures. A main part of the course is to build a line-following car from scrach (maybe not since we've used the Ardurino board for the logic, which did make the project much easier than previous years). And content is mostly interesting (despite the lab demo part, you have to spend days to adjust the parameters to make the car turn just the right angle...).
sections.teaching: The teaching is clear, and the concepts aren't difficult to understand. The tutorial sessions are especially good and I do recommend to participate all of them, since these tutorials do give some tricky questions which do help us to gain better knowledge of the concepts.
sections.grading:
A main part of the grade is the final lab demo, which means you'd better make sure there is nothing wrong with your car before the deadline. The midterms and finals were quite easy (I don't know if others think so too, since I've got full grade in both), and you should be okay once you're familiar with the concepts and the formulas. Below is the grade formation:

LAB assignments: 29% total; first 5 labs 5% each, final lab 4%

quizzes (pop-up quiz in totorials, open book) 3% (you only need to get 6 out of 8 right to earn the full mark, it's very easy so don't worry)

LAB exam: 20% (midterm)

Written exam: 25% (final)

Project demo: 20%

Project report: 3%
sections.workload: Before starting on the final project, the workload is quite low, basically you just have to make sure you've submit the lab assignments on time (the deadline is only a couple hours after your lab session). However, How much time you spend in the final few weeks isn't under your control...

All topics are super easy to understand. It's best if you have PHYS1114 experience. Slightly harder concepts such as adders are not tested during exams or labs, so no worries.

The robotics project component isn't covered extensively during lectures. You will need to handle C++ programming yourself, but the C++ required for this project is much easier than that in COMP2011, so a basic understanding of Python and JavaScript should be sufficient.

Lab exam are just labs, simple.

The final exam is multiple choice, heavily involving KVL and KCL, and features very basic C++ and logic MC questions. If you are good at PHYS1114, this is easy as fuck, so the mean score is high.

Even if you are a Year 1, or even if you haven't studied Physics electives during high school. Just ask AI to help you study, there are secret hacks and skills from AI or from higher-level ELEC electronic courses to make your exam much easier to do, but you'll have to find them yourself. I won't give away those skills freely right here.

sections.grading:
My grade is an A, with an overall score of 95.  
I think the grading is pretty bad, but reasonable.

This course has around 300 students taking it every semester.  
If you look at the mean below, it's so freaking high, and a single score is extremely valuable towards your final grade.  
I guess the median for this course might lie around 83 to 86.

I've heard from others that an overall score of 83 is a C+, and 87 is only a B. That truly sucks.  
Missing a score in a lab, like not getting a bonus score during a lab period, can drop you from an A to an A-.

For the project, if you can finish under 30 seconds, you might get an A+.  
Or, unluckily, if your robotic car fails to reach the end, even if you worked so hard and had successful trials at home but it failed during the demo, you can drop from a 95 (A) to an 85 (probably a B-).  
That's horrible, and it's why this is an extremely competitive course.

I guess this is the course that made a number of students disgusted by the ELEC department and never going to have an ELEC major or ELEC courses in their future.

sections.workload:
Before the project period, the workload consists only of labs, but during the project period, you will have more to do.

Some say the project is a nightmare, but I think it's a common experience. If you want to join the HKUST robotics team, this project should not be a hurdle for you.

As for the project, do not think it's easy or that you can "vibe-code" and generate usable code with AI agents. I've tried it, and it sucked. You truly need to debug deeply and work intensively to make the robots more robust for ALL cases.

I would say that the time I consumed was 10% writing code that WORKS to run the whole map, and 90% debugging and improving robustness. You absolutely need to actively tune the speed to make turns and perform smart sensor identification. Be careful with sensor components; hitting walls at your home can destroy the sensor's metal wires or cause them to bend and break.

The project report is also manageable. Ask your friend to generate a logic diagram, and then you can find some top-tier LLMs to generate entire documents in LaTeX format and receive a free 3 points.

Most importantly, find a good friend as a teammate. It's better if you can direct them to do things if you tend to be leading the project.

sections.content:
The course provides fundamental knowledge in electrical engineering, including the introduction to  basic electronic components and basic circuits such as transistor circuit and H-bridge, PWM control, KCL&KVL, basic logic control, and a little bit Arduino programming.

During the lab session, you will be expected to build electronic circuits, measure the resistance and voltage with multimeter and record your result in the lab assignment. The guidance will be provided on the tutorial sessions.

On the other hand, For the final project, you will design and program a line-tracking robot to autonomously navigate a designated route on the given map. The map is provided (at least, this semester did) and you are allowed to take it back to your dorm for tuning. There will be two test run  so if you fail the first one, don't be so worry cuz you have a second chance.
sections.teaching: The teaching material is well organized, and Mr. SHAO is a kind person who is willing to answer your questions after class.
sections.grading:
Lab assignments: 29%
5% for each first 5 labs; 4% for the last lab
Quizzes: 3%
Pop-on quizzes during tutorial sessions (open book). To get the full 3% points, you should answer 6 questions out of 8 in total correctly.
Exams:
Lab Exam: 20% (close book)
Written Exam: 25% (close book)
Project:
Project demo: 20%
Report: 3%

I didn’t do well on the written exam and only scored 69 out of 100, which made me think I was heading for a bad grade. However, since each component carried a similar weight in the overall score, I still had a chance to redeem myself by doing well in the other parts. In the end, I scored 18 out of 20 on the lab exam, got full marks on my project demo and other graded components, and ended up with an A.
So don’t worry too much if you mess up one part—there’s always room to bounce back.
sections.workload: In the first few weeks, you may feel the workload is light, all you need to do is to attend the lab session on time and finish the assignment. However, once you finish the written exam and start to work on final project, the stituation changes. Please keep in mind that the final project may take you a large amount of time. For me, I spent an entire weekend and several  weekdays afternoon to tune my robot, at the time when final exams and several deadline of the asssignments in other class were just around the corner. So plan your time accordingly.

sections.content: A course that covers the basic components in a circuit (resistor, diode, transistor, H-bridge etc.) and the basic rule for analysing a circuit (KCL KVL). The concepts are quite easy to understand, but can be complex when it comes to calculation. At the end of the course you are required to use all the previous knowledge to build a robot car with one teammate as the final project, you need to keep debugging the car until it is able to follow a rather complex white line track on the mat.

sections.content:
I took this thinking it was an easy A+ course but boy was I wrong.

This course covers basic knowledge on energy, power, circuit connections and calculation, and arduino programming. The concepts are easy to understand, but hard to implement.
sections.teaching:
The teaching is... okay.

The lectures are boring and will not help much. Just study the lecture notes.

The tutorials though, must go. There are quizzes almost every tutorial to strengthen your knowledge and the instructor teaches and explains very clearly.
sections.grading:
If anyone tells you this is a 'good grade course', do NOT believe them, as they are either geniuses who know everything or they're just lying.

Labs: 29%
Quizzes: 3%
Lab Exam: 20%
Written Exam: 25%
Project: Project Demo 20%
Report: 3%

The labs are free, just attend and finish them in time and you'll get full mark, if you don't know how to do something, ask for help and the TAs will guide you through the problem.

Quizzes are still easy, if you study the lecture notes and attend the tutorials (the quizzes are done during tutorials), you'll get full mark easily.

Lab exams, hoho, that's where it starts going downhill. If you have no experience in circuit connection and only rely on the lectures and labs, you're cooked, as what you have to do during the exam is BEYOND harder than that during lab sessions.

Written exams: It's very difficult. You don't have sources except for the two exercises the course provides you with.

Project: The 6 lab sessions essentially help you with building the whole car, so no need to worry about that. But the coding you have to do is a nightmare. Takes a lot of time and effort for trial-and-error. Though the good thing about the project is it gives you two trial days, where on the second (last) trial, the instructor usually lets you off with minor mistakes (skipped a turn, completed the whole map a little slower than required) and gives you full mark.

Report: It's free, just be sure to write everything it tells you to.
sections.workload:
If you don't have pre-existing knowledge on circuit connection and arduino coding, you're cooked.

If you don't have a reliable partner for the project, you're cooked as well.

Everything is fine and has a medium to low workload until the final project (The robot car). Where the slightest deviation in your car's placement or the sensor location can lead to everything failing.

My group's car was running perfectly fine during the test runs, completed the trial with no errors, and under the time limit. But during the first demo, not sure if it was the sensors' problem or the car's placement, it went off the map at the first turn.

This course takes a toll on your well-being both physically and mentally, with physical being the final project taking millions and millions of trial-and-error to finish, and mentally being the car failing at the slightest deviation from its working state.

sections.workload: Most of the workload comes from the robot car. This robot car will make you rage a lot. Make sure that you go to your demo sessions with the same battery level as it was when you had your successful runs in the testing session. Even if you might do that, there is still a possibility that you don't get full marks in the demo sessions. Take our case for example. sections.content: This course teaches the basic rules for electrical engineering such as KCL and KVL with some added in coding for the final project which is a robotic car that you build and code to follow some white line on a mat.
sections.teaching:
Can't say much about the lecture since you can learn most of the knowledge from the lecture notes.
The lecturer for the tutorial do have some Chinese accent which makes it a bit hard to understand but overall it is okay.
The student TAs from the lab are very kind and helpful and are very willing to answer any questions that you have. But there are ONE particular assistant that is very RUDE and are just straight up not giving us any useful advise. All he would do is tell us that we have shorted the circuit and didn't tell us which part of the circuit is wrong. We KNOW that we have built it wrong because we asked him how to FIX it. Instead he just keep shouting at us that we are building it wrong, look at the graph, build it according to the graph.
The lesson of this story is that, if you have any questions regarding your circuits, don't ask the bald guy.
sections.grading:
The lectures does count attendance so you can attend them depends if you have the time. However, there are pop-up quiz during the tutorial which counts for 3% total grade so you may want to attend them all if possible.
There are 6 Lab assignment that you would have to attend for 29% of your total grade. All of them are very simple as if you encounter any difficulties you can simply ask the TA for help. Most of the groups are able to receive bonus marks for all the Lab assignments just remember to hand in the lab sheet before the end of the lessons so that you don't miss the 1 mark for each lab.
The Lab exam counts for 20% towards the final grade and is relatively simple. If you have attended all the Labs, the lab exam won't be that much of a trouble to you and you are likely to get 2 out of the 3 question correct even if you didn't do any revision for the exam.
After or during the mid-term period there will be a written exam which counts for 25% grade. The written exam only has 5 question with each question having 3-4 subquestions, if you messed up at the first subquestions, you better pray that the next question is correct since most of the question are follow-up from the first subquestions. The written exam includes circuit building, KVL, KCL , logic functions and a coding question.
The main point of this course is the robot car that you build with your group mate. This part includes the project demo which is 20% of your grades and the report for the project is 3%. At first you may think this will be a fun and fulfilling project with your friend. But soon you will find out that this little car is a creation from hell and it will only bring frustration and despair. The car has the consistency of a 3 year old in the playground, watching it run the same code three times can have vastly different results. The difference is like a man who works in a steel beam factory with a family and kids, on the other hand is a man who stares at the sun for 3 hours straight when we wakes up and goes out to catch rats to put them in the microwave in a public 7-11. I don't know which one is more preferred but they are very freaking different. But if you and your group mate have a iron will you two may be able to build a code that can adapt to the rat that is your car which can consistently complete the tracks that is specially provided since the mat that was given to you is different from the one used on the exam day. You may think that since you are able to run your car through the mat that is said to be used on the exam, you will be home free right? WRONG, those mats aren't even the same ones that is used on the exam so the testing was actually just pointless. When you put your car on the mat on the exam day you will find out that your car is running differently from the testing run. By then it's already to late to change anything since you are not allow to change your codes during the exam.
Overall this course has some grading issues but it's still a fun experience if you like suffering for 30 hours just to get 11/20.

sections.content:

Next, KCL and KVL are taught and will be used in solving complex circuits. Then, you'll learn the concepts of regulators, transistors, H_bridge, DC motors. After that, boolean algebra, and arduino programming will be taught. After learning all of these important concepts, you and your groupmate will enter the project period, where you have to work on your robot car and test the code numerous times. There are an early demo and a final demo.

The content is generally useful and meaningful. I have learnt so much from this course. I feel like a more practical course like elec1100 is worth it, as you can apply the knowledge from lecture notes to work on your robot car. Its like programming and building circuits.

sections.content:

sections.content:
Lecture topics:
Week 1 Course Introduction and Robot Classification
Week 2 Basic Components, Energy, and Power
Week 3 DC Regulation and Pulse Generation
Week 4 PWM Control
Week 5 Transistors and H-bridge
Week 6 KVL & KCL
Week 7 Sensors and Logic Basics
Week 8 K-map
Week 9 MCU and Arduino
Week 10 Arduino Code

Lab topics:
1. Equipment
2. Diodes and Pulse Generation
3. Transistors and H-bridge
4. Logics
5. Sensors and MCU
6. Assembly of the Car

Most of the content taught in the lectures is not too hard and difficult to understand. There are a decent amount of calculations but they are not too hard and are easy to handle.

Labs from the first couple of weeks are straightforward and teach you how to assemble simple electric circuits. Bonus marks will be given to each lab if you finish all the checkpoints in the given lab manual. You are almost guaranteed to get full marks for each lab if you just follow the lab manual and make sure to do the tasks given to you at a steady pace. The last couple of labs mainly focus on your project, in which you have to build a robot car equipped with sensors tasked to navigate a roadmap. These couple labs will need you to construct the robot car with your partner, and the lab will teach you how to program the robot car. The lectures end early compared to other courses, as there will be a project period where you and your partner will have to work on programming your robot car.

This project is quite tricky as you are mostly going to encounter a decent amount of errors when programming your car, but there will be trial/practice sessions during the project period where you can go test your robot car without counting towards your grades. Just try to attend all the sessions and work on the car with your partner on your free time, and you'll be just fine.

- Lab: 6 Lab Assignments (30% total).
- Quiz: Pop-up In-class Quizzes (open book, 15% total), only the top 70% of your performance will
be counted.
- Exam: Final Written Exam (close book, 30%).
- Project: Project Demo (20%) and report (5%).
sections.teaching: His teaching is decent. Easy to understand and delivers the content quite well.
sections.grading: The grading is fine. If you make sure you follow the lab manuals carefully and avoid making mistakes, you are almost guaranteed to get full marks on the lab sessions. The assignments are pretty easy and simple. The majority of your grade comes from the written test, lab exam, and project demo. So you want to get as much score on those as possible.
sections.workload:
There isn't too much work to do in this course. There were weekly assignments, but they were easy to do and only contained a few questions per assignment, so you'll be able to finish them in no time.

During the project period, you'll have to take some of your time out to program your car with your partner and have to attend the practice sessions as well so may be a little more time consuming but other than that there really isn't that much workload.

sections.content:
lecture包含了KCL,KVL,欧姆定律，二极管，PNP，NPN元件，传感器和基础的逻辑运算。内容非常简单基础，期中之后我就没再听过，看ppt也能看懂，但期末的笔试有一定难度，依然建议去听课。
lab才是这门课的重点，你会在实验室学习使用各种仪器，做一些和lecture有关的实验并最后组装一辆小车。注意！lab是两人一组，包括最后的project，找一个可靠的队友。
tutorial只是讲解实验准备，确保你了解的情况下去不去听课无所谓。
重点强调一下lab，每节lab你都要做数个实验，会有TA帮助你并记录你们的完成状况，两小时内完成所有任务会有bonus分数，这在你熟悉实验内容的情况下并不难。TA人非常好，不要顾忌向他们提问，遇到问题或困难可以请他们帮助。lab的最后几节课会让你拼装一辆小车，这就是你project的小车，组装的牢固一些，不然后面会吃大亏。在project当中，教授会给出一张有白线的地图（这个地图每年都不一样），你需要编程让小车沿着地图上的白线走并完成一些任务。绝对不要小瞧这个project！这看起来不难，但你可能遇到无穷多的问题。我们小组在project环节遇到了许多失败，有时候小车会出现一些无法理解地错误，你如果追求稳定地满分，这会让你抓狂。我们也和别的组讨论了方案，有些人甚至没考虑很多情况，用逻辑存在错误地代码幸运地跑出了满分，这就无关你的努力了。最糟糕地是，教授会安排测试场地，你要去那里才能在地图上测试你的小车。这个测试几乎每天都有一个时间段，周末除外，但测试场地只有三张地图，所有人都要在挤在一个时间段测试，一天基本测不了几次，你的时间只会浪费在无尽的排队上。
sections.teaching: WONG, Man Hoi教授讲的还不错，虽然很多地方他只是在念ppt，但对于重点内容他会讲得很详细，这对期末考试非常有帮助。其他概念你看ppt也能懂。

sections.content: The project of ELEC1100 is a hands-on task which requires students to build a small car and construct the circuit on a breadboard to motivate the car. Key components used in this circuit include nano-board, DC motor, transistor, sensors, etc. The project involves programming the car’s logic using Arduino, allowing the car to track the white line on a black-background map, and turn accurately and perform action at specific positions. Throughout the project, we first need to understand the working functions and principles of each circuit component by individually conducting experiments. Then we learn to write logic code to let the car move due to the map’s layout, using the sensors’ output to control the direction and speed of the wheels. Lastly, in the project demo, we need to let the car move on the map, when passing the specific positions, we gain score, which means the further the car moves on the line, the more score we will get.

sections.content:
Basic electronics and electrical stuff - circuits with diodes, transistors, and logic gates, KCL and KVL. Basic Arduino programming is also covered, which is required in the project. Overall, very rudimentary stuff.

My problem with this course is that its content is too technical for an introductory level and not advanced enough for those seeking in-depth technical knowledge. It covers basic circuitry and electrical knowledge but lacks the depth required to practically apply this knowledge in robotics. Beyond the written test, I don’t see how the content could benefit me in applying the theoretical knowledge in robotics.  

The practical lab sessions could have been enjoyable if not for the bonus mark policy. The policy penalizes students who exceed the two-hour time limit for lab completion by deducting a mark, discouraging students to explore and learn the circuit logic. Even though I wanted to experiment with the circuit and try to understand its inner logic, the bonus mark policy always acted as a deterrent.

In my opinion, if you are genuinely interested in electronics/electrical engineering and robotics, just join the HKUST Robotics or Robomaster team. Despite not getting in the team, I still learned so much more from my experience in Robomaster than this course.

sections.workload:
Before the project, it’s fine. However, it becomes very stressful during the final project period.

The final project is incredibly, incredibly stupid in my opinion for the following reasons.

1. Crowded testing session.
During the 1 week or so of the final project, there were testing sessions every day. However:
-The testing sessions are way too short.
-THERE’S TOO MANY FUCKING PEOPLE. The testing sessions are held in a lecture hall and there are hundreds of people lining up to test their cars and only two maps were provided. This means that you might have to wait in line for twenty minutes just for the car to miss the first turn and you’re left confused and frustrated. What a lot of students ended up doing was that they printed/bought their own map.  

2. To many external factors.  
Even a slight change in sensor sensitivity can result in significant timing differences, affecting your ability to turn correctly. Rather than focusing on improving the code logic, most of the time will be spent on adjusting the sensor sensitivity. Moreover, changes in the battery level also affect the sensor sensitivity and the velocity of the car. So, you must constantly ensure that the battery is fully charged.

Additionally, as I mentioned above, a lot of groups opted to use their own maps. The problem is that the map is usually made of different materials, resulting in different levels of friction of the surface and how reflective the map is. This means you must adjust all the speed and delay values according to the map you’re testing on.  

Honestly why can’t the course instructors just provide every group with the same map? I’m pretty sure everyone is willing to pay for it if it guarantees a consistent result.  

Even with very well written code, the performance can be affected by the placement of the car and its starting direction. I know groups that got 20/20 in the testing sessions who got lower than 10 in the final demo.

Oh, did I also mention that the individual project report, which requires a minimum of 1200 words, is only three percent of your grade? Lol.

If you're already planning on joining the Robotics or Robomaster team, or you want to enjoy the semester without excessive workload, DO NOT TAKE THE FUCKING COURSE.

Lecture:
● The course help you to know and build circuits with diodes, transistors, and logic gates. sections.workload:
There’s very light workload in the weeks before the final projects, but it becomes a nightmare during the project period.

To make your car navigate the course accurately, you need precise control. However, it's nearly impossible to control the car very precisely.

1. The velocity and direction of the tires can't change instantly, and you need repeatedly trials to find the correct parameters (velocity, time) to let the car perform a good turn.

2. External factors, like changes in lighting or collision with the sensors, can disrupt the car's performance. Even slight variations in the light source or sensor sensitivity can result in significant  differences in the performance.

3. The drop in battery level with repeated tests will affect your car's behavior as well. If you are not charging very often, you may find all your adjustments are based on a gradually decreasing speed.

4. Unexpected issues except these may also arise, such as where and how you place the car on the starting line. The variation on the car's starting direction may also affect its performance.

If you decide to enroll in this course, you'd better pray for luck to  your car. All students have to suffer a lot before they update their devices.

sections.content:
I will write from the perspective of a student without any background knowledge in electrical or robotics.

Regarding the lectures:
1. The course covers various fundamental electrical components, including capacitors, diodes, resistors, and so on.
2. Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL) and Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL) will be taught.
3. The lectures will cover topics such as H bridges, PWM, and logic gates.
4. Basic programming for Arduino using the C language will be introduced.

Regarding the labs:
1.  The labs will focus on teaching students how to use basic electrical equipment, such as power supplies, function generators, multimeters, and Digital Storage Oscilloscopes.
2. Students will learn how to assemble a line follower robot, which will serve as the final project for the course.

Regarding the tutorials:
1. The tutorials will help students prepare for the lab sessions.

Personal Feelings:
All the contents are very basic, only thing u need to do is to read the lab guidline before lab and pay attention in class. Thats it.
sections.teaching:
Both professors have a deep understanding of the subject matter they are teaching. They have a comprehensive knowledge base and stay updated with the latest developments in their field. This allows them to provide accurate and up-to-date information to their students.

They are able to effectively communicate complex concepts in a clear and understandable manner. They break down difficult topics into manageable parts, using relatable examples and analogies to enhance comprehension. They adapt their teaching style to cater to different learning styles and ensure that all students can grasp the material.

anyhow, very chill teaching style
sections.grading:
Quiz (10%): grade is based on the best 14 out of 20 questions.

Lab (30%): ez 30% .

Lab exam (15%): Full marks (15) for me, and the mean is around 10.XX (I don't remember the exact number).

Written exam (20%): I scored 50 out of 100 on the written exam, which is lower than mean. I didn't study at all and spent the entire night playing games before the exam.

Final project (20%): For my final project, I remember my robot car successfully completed a full run on the first trial. However, I didn't take the practice trials seriously afterward. I received full marks in the early demo. The Arduino coding was simple, and if you don't understand something, you can ask your friends for suggestions.

Final Report (5%): The final report is an easy 1200-word assignment. Just meet all the requirements, and you will receive full marks. It doesn't require too much effort.

Final Grading: I received an A- with a score of 90 out of 100. This is why I believe this is the easiest course you can take in your first year. Even if you score below the mean on the exam, you can still achieve an A-range grade. Can you find a similar course like this at UST?

As an engineering student, this is a basic skill you should possess (debugging and imaging). If you find yourself struggling with the final project, perhaps you should consider pursuing a science-related field where paper exams are more prevalent.

Introduction about robots. Both hardware and software are included.

The course includes lectures, tutorials and labs. The content of tutorials are preparing for labs and they help a lot, so make sure you attend all the tutorials, unless you are quite confident about labs.

For the project part, you will need to build a robot car and write some code. The goal is to make the robot car follow a UST-shape path and complete some tasks. It's not difficult, but you need to spend time on debugging your code. There will be coding test sessions for you to test your robot car's behavior before the demo.

For the project part, I spent about 3 days (~8 hours in total), including writing code and debugging both software and hardware. It may be annoying sometimes, but you will get a great sense of achievement when you see your robot car completes the demo. Generally speaking, the project is quite interesting for me.

Don't be afraid of making mistakes. Actually, I burned 2 ICs and 1 battery monitor XD, but finally got a good grade. I would say making mistakes is also part of this course, and I gained a lot from them. Also, TA and peer mentors offered great help in the course. Feel free to ask them when you meet problems and you will find the course not so hard.

sections.grading:
The distribution for this semester can be found in other reviews so I'll skip it ;)

I suppose people who takes this course want to get into A range so objectively speaking, the grading is around average. For this semester, if you would like to get into A range, you'll need 95% or above(Source: Professor).

Some people may say it is easy to attain those marks, with the first argument that lab marks are free

Sure, if you have a good partner, or else good luck because for my case I got a non-chalant partner who never did any preparation before lab and always come to lab sleepily, and for most labs, I was able to make it 1 or 2 mins before the bonus score is gone.

Lab exam and written exam (I'll skip the common knowlege that exam require to be careful). For me, the thing I found I am most unfamiliar with is diode stuff so I'll give the advice of making sure that you understand how diodes will interact in A.C. circuits.

Things I agree with:
The project is easier than it seems as I was able to finish the project successfully with my partner doing absolutely nothing :)

Quizes are free marks if you pay attention to lesson

Things you should put all your focus in:
Lab Exam: 15/15
Written Exam: 89/100

Things you shouldn't be worried about if you have a partner who wants to get good grade:
Lab: Not 30/30 :)

Things you shouldn't be worried about:
Quiz: 10/10
Project: 25/25

Final Grade: B+ (94.X%)
Good luck to you guys and pray that you may achieve A range if you take this course
sections.workload:
Objectively speaking, the couse has a light workload.

Lectures:
During the semester, I'll just preview the lecture notes before the lecture(which should take you around 10-30mins depending on you speed and amount of lecture material you are less familiar with)

Labs:
For every lab, due to my circumstances, I'll write down every step I need to take on a text file, always see if the Lab Summary has any calculations that can be done before the lab and fill in any blank that is fillable and use tinkercad to try building the circuit. If you want to get full mark in lab, this is the safest way to achieve it [ofc having a gd partner always >> these extra effort =) ]

Project: (I suggest you refer to other reviews as I had to solo this)
For me, I attended almost every coding session possible in the first week (Missed two session as I did not want to skip too much lectures for this as well). So, it approximately took me 10-12 hours(Note: I had very little experience with arduino coding and the time includes time testing outside the testing session) and I was able to get the 20 mark perfect run in the early demo.  

There isn't much to comment about the written report as it is simply a report that requires you to take some time to reflect about your experience.

So again if you have a decent partner, the workload should be very light.

ELEC1100 旨在提供電氣工程的基礎知識、基本電子元件以及機器人及其子系統的設計、實施和評估所需的技能。
它涵蓋了基本的電子工程原理和技術。
提供實作實驗室課程，並輔以講座和教程，讓學生對電子工程原理有系統的了解。

分級是瘋狂的，但在某種程度上是合理的。
大多數人都能在 Quiz、report 和 Lab 中獲得滿分，這意味著它們非常簡單。此外，本次SEM中的項目非常簡單，它為您提供了大量的時間來檢查您的編碼以運行您的汽車。因此，獲得 A 範圍的關鍵是在考試（實驗室和筆試）中獲得 90% 左右，

sections.content:
Starts from basics of electronics, such as voltage, power and circuit analysis via KCL/KVL.

Moves onto specific theory which will be required in creating the robot. H-bridges, voltage regulator ICs, NPN/PNP transistors, motors etc.

Final few weeks are spent applying what is learnt in building a path following robot.
sections.teaching:
The pacing isn't great.

The first few weeks are spent teaching things which are super basic.

The lecture notes in transistors aren't great, go to youtube to understand some of the more difficult electronics, what they do and how they work etc.
sections.grading:
Grading is fair and transparent.

There are lab assignments and quizzes in class which test knowledge.

The midterm is based on breadboard skills. There is a final project which involves building a robot and making it follow a path.
sections.workload:
Relatively low. Appropriate for a 3 credit course.

During the robot-building weeks, may be required to spend a lot more time than expected. The midterm and labs/quizzes don't require too much attention. (can focus on math1014 haha)

It is a good intro course for electronic engineering. Be aware though, ELEC study further down the line, if you so choose ELEC, will be MUCH more mathematically rigorous.
This course is an intro ENGINEERING course, but electronic engineering foundation courses atleast, require a deep study of the theory behind electronics physics and signals,systems etc.

Try and pick up as much as you can and be an active participant in the robot building phase, nobody likes a lazy partner.

sections.content:
Course Description

ELEC1100 is designed to provide the fundamental knowledge in electrical engineering, basic electronic components and skills needed for the design, implementation and evaluation of a robot and its subsystems.
It covers the basic electronic engineering principle and techniques.
Hands-on laboratory sessions, complemented with lectures and tutorials, are provided to allow students to have a systematic view of the electronic engineering principles.
Students apply the knowledge and principles learnt to design and build a functional robot by themselves.

This course is about basic electric circuits
propositional logic,boolean algebra, KVL,KCL,Arduino programming.

For example, my teammate is a kind Korean exchange student, she's pretty good at doing lab and writing codes.

ELEC1100 is designed to provide the fundamental knowledge in electrical engineering, basic electronic components and skills needed for the design, implementation and evaluation of a robot and its subsystems.

It covers the basic electronic engineering principle and techniques.
Hands-on laboratory sessions, complemented with lectures and tutorials, are provided to allow students to have a systematic view of the electronic engineering principles.

Students apply the knowledge and principles learnt to design and build a functional robot by themselves.

sections.content:
Quite easy, you don't need to review it after class because you can understand the concepts during the class or by learning by yourself before class.
Contents involve commonly used electronic components, from diodes to transistors. Also involves KCL and KVL calculation, H-bridge, resistors, and some basic ICs. Later on in the course, they teach us Arduino.

The final project involves building a robot car that follows a white line 'UST' on a black mat with an Arduino Nano board as the control unit. It needs good manipulative skills to build the robot car because some parts of your car may be broken down when you are testing. And you may own a demanding patient because the robot car is quite annoying. You can run your code normally yesterday but today your code may not run well due to many reasons.

sections.content:
The whole course is based on making a robotic car that can traverse a track.

You will learn about different circuit components(at a very very basic level)

Topics that will prepare you for the final project would be
- Circuit components(Resistors, capacitors, diodes, and transistors)
- Kirchoffs Voltage and Current Laws, which are pretty much just conservation of energy laws for circuits
- car components(motors & pulse width modulation,  sensors, Arduino, H-bridge and inverter Integrated circuits at a basic level)
- Boolean logic, algebra, De Morgans law (no k map which is disappointing and I highly recommend self studying
- combinational logic(which uses the very basic logic gates)
- coding in C/C++

Over all, this course is so fun.

The labs are a bit hard at first, but once you get used to the equipment and basic design thinking, its relatively easy to complete each lab in under 2 hours.

I dropped by one of Qiao Shiming's lectures, and he spoke like a robot, so err yeah I don't recommend Qiao Shiming. Prof Ki is also a good teacher, also good humour too, but I'd still say that I'd recommend Profession Shen as first choice of teacher tho.

The only two tricky parts for this course are mid-term and final project.  If your car cannot complete the run, say it veered off route
at the second corner, you will only get around 14/20. In other courses, it may just be the difference of one subgrade. But in this course, it will be the matter of a whole grade, A+ to B+!!!

But, there's time for you to adjust your final project on the real examination route before real exam. If you spend enough time there shouldn't be any problem on getting full score. ( And there's four trials, every trial counts. You can gamble on your luck)

sections.content:
teaches basic electronics and Arduino car coding

week 1~6 (lecture 1~12) ACHUTAVARRIER PRASAD, Vinod teaches basic electronics, the resistance, KCL, KVL, is similar to those in PHYS 1114. there are also transistors, capacitors but just the simple part of it.
week 7~8 (lecture 13~15) YANG, Yansong teaches simple arduino code and simple line following robot things.

week 2~7: one lab assignment per week. it is based on what they have taught in the lecture so it is simple. the TA will teach you how to do it in tutorials. lab assignments is checked by your 4~5 pages (mostly screenshots that takes up many spaces) pdf file and Tinkercad simulation shown in the lab session. 2 hours will be enough to complete the lab.

week 9~12: project demo and report. (no lectures, no tutorials, only lab sessions) 2 light sensors (1/0) line follower Arduino robot. 1 light sensor faces the front as obstacle detection.
Full online semester so we submit our code, TA upload your code to their robot, and show the result to you through Zoom. So, you only get limited number of trials.
Therr are 4 weeks of testing, each week 2 code versions, each version 2 trials = 16 trials in total. (the 2 code versions are submitted before testing so you can't modify the second code version after testing the first one. So, one small error may cost you 4 trials)

sections.workload:
two separate 1 hour lectures, a 1 hour tutorial and a 3 hours lab session per week is what written in the time table of the course.

However, there are just 8~9 weeks of lectures (one normal semester has 12~13 weeks). Tutorial teaches you how to finish your lab assignment, which you can just skip it. And you just need to use 5 minutes in the 3 hours lab session to show your lab assignment to the TA and you are free to go. the workload is really light.

sections.content: The content of this course is straightforward. You learn about components of the robot that will ultimately lead you to the final project. We covered topics like electronic components, energy, KCL & KVL, DC power, transistor, H-bridge, PWM control, sensors, logics, and the Arduino code. The powerpoint given makes the content extremely easy to follow.
sections.teaching: The lectures are a little boring but since they are only 50 minutes, it is tolerable. Professor Murch's voice is clear but some of the content might be covered too fast it is hard to understand. The professor will always ask if we have any questions and replies to emails quickly. The powerpoint slides are great and if you miss any lectures you would most likely still understand the content. My TA is Yi Meng and she recaps what is taught in the lectures and prepare us for the labs.
sections.grading:
Lab: 6 Lab Assignments (30% total).
Quiz: Pop-up In-class Quizzes (open book, 10% total), online submission in iPRS (20 questions in total, only the top 60% answers will be counted).
Exam: On-line Exam (close book, 35%).
Project: Project Demo (20%) and Report (5%).

The lab was extremely easy to complete as answers are provided in the powerpoint in the tutorials. Most students get a full score here. For the pop quizzes, if you pay attention to the lectures, you should do fine. As for the exam, I thought I prepared well but I still find it challenging. The exam was divided into MCQ, FRQ, and Tinkercad circuit test. For the last part, it is either you get the points or not and it is worth 20 percent of the test. I forgot to put a wire to connect the GND to GND which costed me 20 marks. The project is also a complete nightmare. You are supposed to write a code for a robot to make it complete the tasks and earn points. However, much of the part is based on luck since various factors can affect how much your robot performs and there's only a few chances you can debug your code and test it out. It really depends on luck if your robot works. I used the same code many times and got different results. You also need to write a report at the end.

My scores:
Lab: Full
Quiz: Full
Exam: 47.67/100 (mean: 71.40, SD: 20.09)
Lab: 18/20
Report 5/5

Turns out I got a B-. I think the grading is pretty good considering my extremely poor exam score. Overall, the content of the course is interesting. However, if you aim for a great score and don't want to suffer with the project, don't choose it.
sections.workload: The workload is average for a 4 credit course. There is a lab that you have to complete every week. I think it should take around 2 hours. The professor might also release some homework for practice but it is not required that you submit it. The worst part would be stressing about the project since there's only a few chances to test the code and you really have to make sure that there are no mistakes. The project report has a minimum of 1200 words. You can finish it in one day.

sections.content: There's nothing much new. The course starts with NSS Physics circuit things like P=IV, V=IR stuff and building circuits. Then introduced a few more things like diodes, transistors, and then introduced audrino and sensor thingy and proposition logic. Most importantly, you need to "build" a car following their step-by-step guide and write a code for the car to complete the objectives. A fun course, especially because the part of physically building a car was skipped due to pandemic
sections.teaching: The instructor delivered the content quite clearly. In fact, even if you cannot understand the content, there exist plenty of internal resources that you can look up for without seeking any additional help. Even idiots can understand the knowledge if they are willing to put in some time and effort.
sections.grading: The number score is quite easy to obtain, as there are 55% from projects in total, and you can get at least 30% as long as you have at least one brain cell that can help you understand their step-by-step lab instructions. However, the letter grade is not as cash money as you think. I got 84.5/100 in this course, and its only a B. It is safe to assume that you need at least 90% for A range, which reduces a lot of room of error
sections.workload: Given that this course carries 4 credits, the workload is actually very little, even less than most 3 credit courses, as you only need to spend like a couple hours for the labs each week. More importantly, the course only lasted for around 2/3 of the semester, so the total workload is further reduced

sections.grading:
iPRS 15%
Project Report 5%
Project Demo 20%
Labs 30%
Final (but taken at the end of midterm period) 30%

I got 95.25% overall and A-. I got full marks in every items except for the final. So the grading is pretty crazy! The contents are just too easy that everyone got very high marks. I think you need to get 97% to get an A and nearly 100% to get A+.

I think it would be better if they increase the weighting on the project and project report. Everyone spent so much time on the project yet it weights less than the labs just makes no sense. There are so many to write in the project report but it only contributes 5% to the total grade, and it seems that as soon as you have included everything requires in the project report then you get full points. As a result, everyone got full points in every items and your grade only depends on the exam.

Good grade or not really depends on what you expect. If you are satisfied with B+ or A-, then it would be a leng grade course!

sections.content:
Very easy. Even middle school students can handle it. (I'm not kidding)

Just some very basic electrical knowledge. There are some scary-sounding names like KCL and KVL, but surprisingly simple.

It does require some programming, but it's still easy. My only programming background is the "turtle" thing, even not Python turtle, and that's enough to program the control logic of a robot car.  

I didn't have any C++ background, and even didn't do any self-learning. I just simply imitated the sample code given by prof and achieved Perfect Run with "if/else" conditional statements.
sections.teaching: The teacher has a mainland accent, which is just what I look forward to, because it's not easy for me to understand native English.
sections.grading:

sections.workload:

sections.content: The first few lectures of the course are similar to what we were taught in high school physics, basically some calculation and concepts about electric circuit, voltage and current. In the later part , some more new concepts are introduced such as KCL and KVL, transistors and PWM control, but overall it should be easy to follow and is quite fun to learn about.
sections.teaching: The professor is a cool dude, although his Indian accent could be difficult to follow.
sections.grading:
The grading was insane, like really really insane. According to other comment , it seems like u would need a overall of 96% in  order to get to A range, which means that the margin of error is basically zero, on top of that, the project was kinda a RNG, the same set of codes can produce drastically different result anytime. Use myself as an example, we have been through tons and tons of hardware issue like the the fuse was burnt out, the screw were not tightened and the wheels not being in sync, which already put us in a giant disadvantage. The fun doesn't stop there, during the final session, the luck wasn't on our side, by an inch of nail, we went from potentially getting 18/20 to just 14/20.

Back to the grading, it was insane. I was above mean in the final, with all other stuff except the project getting near full marks, with the 14/20 in the project, it makes to about 88% in the overall course mark. Guess what, it only gets me a B-, not even B+ by nearly 90%, but B-, it was insane!!!!!!!!!
sections.workload: The workload was light at the early part of the semester as there was no assignment , one thing to be mentioned tough is that there would be a lab every week, dealing with the component and the circuit could be time -consuming and frustrating at times, but if you are into those stuff, you might find that interesting. However, it was intense at the end of the semester , you are required to finish a coding project , which takes up a majority of your time. We were allowed to test our codes every day , building your code is already not a easy job, the major issue tough is that only 3 project mats are provided every testing session, so we basically have to wait for eternity in order to go through one trial, as a result, all our times were taken up to the point that we even have to skip other lectures to deal with the project.

sections.content:

Students apply the knowledge and principles learnt to design and build a functional robot by themselves.

sections.content:
Lectures in the first month are pretty simple for students who have basic E&M understanding in secondary school, consisting of content about AC/DC, voltage, current, resistance. Then it moves onto more advanced electronic stuff like PWM, transistors, H-bridge, KCL & KVL, logic gates, and K-map.

While lectures focus on concepts, and sometimes it would be more like a physics class.
Tutorials mostly teach how labs are done and most importantly contain examples for the circuit arrangements. There will be the detail connection information on every single wire on the breadboard which makes it extremely easy to connect the wire in the lab.

Average.
SHAO himself has great and deep understanding on ELEC, but maybe the content of the class restricted his lecture.

- Final Project

An interesting introductory course to EE, you can learn about electronic circuits and a little bit of programming.

Lectures: Attendance is compulsory because there is an iPRS quiz (2 questions) almost every lesson, but most of them are very straightforward. Read the slides before the lectures and you should be good to go.

Tutorials: Focused on preparing us for the next lab. Didn't attend most of them but the slides are useful enough.

Midterm(online, on canvas): Additional exercises and past paper with solutions are provided for midterm preparation. The exam itself is not hard, questions similar to the past paper provided. One minor issue is that you can't return to the last question after you have completed a question (i.e. can't skip questions). This could be somewhat painful especially when doing MCQs.  

Lab: 2 in a group. The tasks aren't too difficult, just remember to read the lab instructions beforehand and refer to the tutorial slides for breadboard arrangements.

Project: Build a line following car. Same groupmate as the lab sessions. There are early and final demo for grading (4 trials each demo), only the trial with the highest mark will be counted. 18/20 for a perfect run, 20/20 only if the perfect run is achieved within 25 seconds. The base logic of the car is quite simple, but expect to handle a lot of edge cases when testing your car on the actual track. A project report (>1200 words) should be submitted after the final demo.

sections.grading:
You have do one labs like every weeks. These labs are quite easy to finish but you still need a hour to finish it. The tutorial will solve most of the difficulties, and you can finish it after some testing and modification.

The final are also acceptable. The questions are not hard to answer if you have do revision.

The pop-up quiz are annoying I would say. You have participate every lesson as you may miss these pop-up quiz if you absent for that lesson.

The car coding, which contain 35% marks, is a disaster. You can get extremely different result with same codes. My car move backward in the first time and run out of control quickly in the second time. Even the demo from the professors themselves requires three time to complete.

So, if you believe yourself as a lucky person, you are welcome to join such gambling. As a result, my report of this demo even have higher mark than my demo.

***I join this course during the Covid-19, not sure is there any difference compared to last few years

There are 6 labs in total; you have to build some circuits by TinkerCad. You have to show the results to the TA. Basically, you can get full marks if you follow the tutorial notes carefully. Also, you get 1 mark by submitting the summary sheet for every lab.

There are 4 pop-up quizzes in total. The 3 highest score will be regarded as the final result. All the questions are MCs.

The final exam is divided into 3 parts, MCs, Long Questions and circuit building. It is not an open book exam, and using the calculator is not allowed.

Well, as long as you spend some effort on this course, you are likely to get some marks. WHAT REALLY MATTERS IS THE FINAL PROJECT
you get 1% as long as you hand in the source code.
4% of the score depends on the report (as long as it meets all requirements, you get full marks).
20% of the score depends on how far can your car reach. Many students fail to get desirable marks in this part (very few information is given before the Demo session). Therefore, even though you perform badly in the exam and pop-up quizzes, you can get a good grade if you perform this well.

For my case:
Labs: 29/30% (Remember to submit the summary sheet ...)
Quiz: 9/15% (I guess the average is about 11-12)
Exam: 18/30% (I got 61/100 and the average is 67)
Project: 20/25%
And I got B+ as the final grade.
As long as your car work, you get a good grade.

Better have some programming background before you join this course.

sections.content:
Basic electronic engineering, course separated into two halves, with the first half being electronic circuits (diodes, transistors and such), and the second half being Arudino programming.

Both were quite interesting, and were not very difficult as well especially if you have prior programming knowledge. The only difficult part of the course was KVL/KCL, and for that I suggest watching some youtube videos explaining them, in particular the video made by Organic Chemistry Tutor which explains it better than the lectures or the notes can.
sections.teaching:
Teaching was decent, Professor Shen did have an accent but was overall clear in speaking and explained ideas well enough, the lecture powerpoints are detailed and explained course concepts clearly, lectures were a bit boring but were mandatory because of the in class pop-up quizzes.

Tutorials were simple and the TA just tells you what to do for the labs, Fox explained the labs and projects extremely well in the tutorials (the circuits for the labs are pretty much given to you completed, so you just recreate it in tinkercad...)

Labs were arranged very well with TAs checking your circuit, which takes only about 10 minutes of waiting and demoing only takes a minute.

Online exam: held a few weeks after the middle of the semester, tests the entire syllabus. 3 parts, part 1 is 10 MCQs, part 2 is a long question based on KVL/KCL, part 3 is building a circuit in tinkercad. Acceptable difficulty, mean is around 69/100.

Labs: build a circuit following the tutorial and finish the lab report, very easy, most students can get full marks on this.

Quiz: 4 in lecture pop-up quizzes over iPRS, quiz area based on recent lectures, 10 questions, given 1-2 minutes for each question, very nerve wrecking as you cannot go back and the time is short.

Project: The worst part of the course, you make a robot car that tracks a line. You have only 4 attempts to test your code, so if you are unlucky, or are the type of person that needs to test your code, prepare to do very poorly.

Project report: 4 page report based on the project, including graphs, logic tables and such.

Got mean overall (68/100), therefore got a B-, expected according to UST standards. Again, the project process was a mess, therefore you shouldn't take this until f2f.

Rated at a B because while workload is heavy, it's pretty good for a 4 credit course.

Popup quizzes: Mostly OK, study the notes a little bit before the quizzes and you will do fine (Very nerve-wrecking to be limited to 1-2 minutes per question though...)

Labs: almost no workload, recreate the circuit given to you in the tutorial in tinkercad, and finish the lab report which takes 30 minutes at most once per week.

Online exam: acceptable, the exam doesn't cover a lot of area since its held about a month after the midterms, split into 3 parts, MCQs which were quite difficult, a long question regarding KCL/KVL, and a circuit building question that just asks you to build a circuit in tinkercad.

Project: Hardest part and also the worst part of the course, you only have 2 chances to test your code, once during the test, and once during the FINAL demo, there is no other chance to test your code, which is absurd. Therefore in the end most people got less than 5/20 with only a few people getting more than half.

Project report: Just follow the guidelines given to you and it would be easy, but do make sure you fulfill ALL the requirements as listed in the guidelines.

sections.teaching:
Shen Shaojie has a solid knowledge in this area, as you can find some introductions of him on web. His accent is relatively good, and as he speaks slowly, you can easily understand him. I think sometimes he doesn't know how to express himself, so there maybe some pauses, but it won't affect anything.

My TA is FOX, he seems strict but actually he is a very nice guy. He will respond to your emails very quick and explain things clearly to you. Also this sem, the final project was unable to hold f2f, but FOX has done everything he could to ensure a fair environment. Though I didn't get a satisfying mark in project, but I think he've done an excellent job.
sections.grading:
Grading Scheme:
- 6 Labs, 6 * 5% = 30%
- 3 Quizzes, 3 * 5% = 15%
- 1 Written exam, 30%
- 1 Project, 20%
- 1 Project report, 5%

For labs, we did it on Tinkercad, which is easy to get used to. Each lab, they'll give you detail descriptions of what you're supposed to do and during Tutoiral lessons, FOX will explain more and even show you the correct circuit for your reference. You need to assemble your circult before lab lessons and during Lab lessons, you need to share screen and show your work to TA, and after demonstration, you need to submit a simple report, the skeleton has already done for you and you only need to put some screenshots inside. This part is easy to get full mark.(sometimes they don't give full mark for report, e.g. 0.95/1, but it doesn't matter)

For quizzes, it appears randomly in the last 10 minutes of a lecture, so you need to pay attention if you usually skip the lecture. The problems are easy and the grading is amazing. There'll be 4 quizzes and each quiz has 5 MC problems, but each problem worths 25 points, meaning that if you answer 4 problems correctly then you'll get full mark. And best 3 of 4 quizzes will be counted. Very easy to get full.

For written exam, the problem is a bit harder this year, but only if you understand lecture slides well, there won't be much trouble. This sem the exam was arranged on Canvas, the order of questions is random and as long as you switch to next problem, you are unable to modify previous answers. So some students were worried and didn't get good mark since they met difficult problems at the beginning, which definitely affect moods.

For project, you need to write the Arduino code of a car and let it run along the white line on the ground. The Arduino code obeys C/C++ syntax so it'll be much easy if you known C/C++ before. Two code test sessions has been arranged and during each session you can submit two versions of codes and TA will upload your code into the car and run it on the map. Unlike computer program, the car didn't run exactly the same each time, as there'll be many factors that can affect its preformance. So even though your code is completely correct, sometimes you'll also get a low mark. And that happens on myself, which is a pity. Actually no one can ensure the result, but this is the best way that TA can do so do not complain.

For the report, you need to describe what you've done in project and describe your code's logic by using flow chart and true tables. As long as you do it as required, you'll get full mark.

My score:
- Labs: 28.95/30 (I think I've done all of them right, and maybe sometimes they don't give full mark, but I'm not sure)
- Quizzes: 15/15
- Written exam: 100/100, Mean 66.55/100, SD 16.52/100
- Project: 6/20
- Report: 5/5
Grade: A
sections.workload:
Workload is not heavy at all. The labs are easy, as detailed instructions have been given. So it only takes less than 1 hour to finish your circuit and reports.
For final project, if you're familier with C/C++, then programming is easy for you. But you need to think a lot for designing the logic and think about special conditions as much as possible and this may takes a long time. 1~2 Weeks required.
There's not much new knowledge in lecture slides, so basically you don't need to spend lots of time for preparing the written exam.

From basic electronics like breadboards, components to IC, logic, K-map, and C++ (Arduino, but that's not much different) the course does not dive deep into them.

What's worse, you have only one chance to test your code before the 'real' demo and that is horrible!

sections.content:
Pretty OK.

Basically a slightly advanced version of secondary school circuitry. Introduces new circuit stuff like transistors, diodes, capacitors, logic gates, timers, etc but not much calculation for those is required (you can always follow the given equations)

Also introduces some circuitry calculation/planning concepts like KVL/KCL and K-map. Nothing too hard tho.

The whole goal of the course is to give your the minimum knowledge to make a robot-controlling circuit board (+ program), so not much is really taught in depth.
sections.teaching:
Meh.

Professors and TAs tend to be pretty helpful (at least this time around) because of the difficulty in building circuitry without a physical circuit.

There's nothing particularly bad about the teaching method, it's just hindered by the fact that this course had to be online and labs are just "connect the dots in this simulation website" plus a bit of paperwork.
sections.grading:
It's not hard to get to B+ if you basically grasped everything in the course. The real challenge comes from the fact that the robot trials are done "online" (remotely by sending your program to the TAs and let them run by themselves).

Welcome to the biggest Online Casino of HKUST.

You are only given 5 trials, 3 different submission attempts and no other possible way of testing whether your robot works in real life. You can make it work in theory, which gives you 14/20 points (20% of final grade), but the rest depends on whether your robot is lucky enough to not bug out when running through the track. Otherwise comes the nondeterministic filter that separates lucky A-rangers from the unlucky B-or-less grades. (Unless you do exceptionally well in the "written" exam)

If you really aim for A range, this course is not for you.
sections.workload:
It's less "heavy workload" but "unfair correlation between workload and actual grade". The workload is pretty light. 6 labs (basically connecting the dots, as said above), 1 homework (which is decent as a practice) and the final project (and PRS).

Since there is no way to test your project in real life (other than buying the circuits yourself or spending the trials), the project (which takes a good portion of the grading) doesn't really reward based on effort, but on luck.

I'd rather have a heavier workload than have a result that I couldn't have controlled.

4.transistors and H-bridge
