8. basic programming knowledge for embedded programming using Arduino

All the things besides sequential logic and programming will be covered in the lab midterm, written exam.
All the things covered in the lecture are VERY USEFUL in the final project.
The first lab familiarizes you with the lab equipment like the DC power source, function generator, and oscilloscope (which are VERY COOL)!

Project proposal (which should be report under normal circumstances)(30%)

For the lab midterm, just go through the review questions and lecture notes. Be CAREFUL when you are building the circuit and make measurements frequently, otherwise, you might lose tons of points.

The written exam covers everything taught in lectures besides the programming stuff.  Go through review questions and past papers, especially those about KCL and KVL. I lost most of my points on KCL and KVL but still get a score slightly above 90.

The lab assignments are lab reports that require you to take measurements and do simple math. It should be submitted before the lab section ends. You can take most of the points as long as you follow the steps in the lab manual. I highly recommend read the lab manual before the lab so that you can have adequate time for debugging.

The pop-up quizzes are very easy. Just make sure you can understand the concepts on the lectures notes.

The final project demo (proposal this term) is what makes the difference in grades. Many people lose points because of the final demo. Make sure your robot can satisfy the requirements with different voltage!

I get a score slightly above 90 in lab midterm and written exam, and I get most of the points from other sections! I get an A in this course.

sections.content:
This is an introductory course on electronics and robotics and suitable for any students with Physics or engineering background. It is generally separated into the theory and practical section, with theory lessons supporting the practical project.
The theory part contains the following topics: Electronic equipments, DC and AC power, PWM (Pulse width modulation) control, H-Bridge and Transistors, Kirchoff's Laws, Sequential logic and Arduino Programming. There will be a written exam at the end of term assessing understanding of above topics so revising is recommended.
The contents learned from above topics also have to be applied to program an electronic robot car to run on a designated track without error, built from scratch, for the practical project. The demo of robot car on the track will take a large portion of the final grade.
While contents are very basic, students with programming and/or Physics background will find it much easier to understand.
sections.teaching:
The professor is very professional and knows the content very well. He's also very enthusiastic, welcoming to questions and constantly invite students to approach him. Having said that, the contents taught in lectures are quite irrelavent to the project.
In contrast, the tutorials are not very useful as they only provide a guideline to your practical work in lab sessions, which can be easily read from the lab manuals. However, the tutorial session before project demo is very useful and worth attending as it provide tips to score well and dealing with problems in the project demo.
sections.grading:
20% from lab mid-term, assessing practical skills with electronic components.
20% from written exam, assessing theory knowledge from lectures.
20% from lab assignments, 30% from project demo and report. As project has to be worked in lab, lab attendance is strongly recommended for good grades.
10% from iPRS questions in lecture.
Groups can join the mini-contest if they score 20/25 in project demo, and by winning it you're guranteed A. Competition is tough, do not expect to win easily.
sections.workload:
The theory part is not difficult for students with Physics or electronics background, so not too much studying is needed.
The project however takes long time and hard work to fine tune the car to ensure it could perform well in the project, therefore the workload is quite high.

sections.content: A project oriented course. It teaches all the knowledge you need to have in order to build and program an autonomous vehicle and also the theories behind, including basic electronics, PWM, transistors, sensors, KCL&KVL, logics, K-map, Truth table, and arduino programming. The content overall isn't really difficult.
sections.teaching:
Prof. Song is a good teacher, he explained things super clearly and interestingly.
He tries his best to make the lecture as interesting as possible and tries his best to interact with his students.

The last lecture was no longer about the course but more about coaching about university life and career for students.
sections.grading:
Grading content :
Lab
Lab Midterm
Final Project
Final Exam
Quiz in class
Final project report

it is easy to get full mark on lab, lab midterm, quiz, report.
you need a little effort for final exam and final project and you will get full mark
sections.workload:
the workload is not really much. you need to finish the final project and do the programming. And at last, you just need to make the final report based on the final project.

The amount of debugging that you might need for your lab project depends on the overall complexity and also how well you've designed the logic.

overall, the workload is not really heavy.

sections.content:
18 Lectures, every lecture has 1 or 2 quizzes

6 Labs, attend minimum 4 labs to be eligible to do the final project

The project is to make a car that could follow and finish a certain track given to you by using all the components and knowledge that you know in the whole course

We use Arduino to program the car instead of doing it using hardware only to do all the logics
sections.teaching:
The professor and all the TAs are good at teaching and know their stuff. They are also approachable and feel comfortable around students so we could ask questions or just have a little. chat with them.

During lab, most of the TAs are friendly and willing to help you if you really can't solve a problem by yourself (debugging not giving answers).
sections.grading:
Grading is very good
20% Lab Mid term
20% Lab assignments (6 labs)
10% Quiz in every lecture (only highest 70% will be counted)
25% Final Project
5% Project report

There is a mini-contest for the final project that you might want to participate and win. If you win, you will be guaranteed to have an A as your grade.
sections.workload:
Little workload at the beginning, no homework. However, near the end of the course we have to do lots of stuffs to finish the final project

The time you spend on the projects really affect the result of your project. You need to find and spend quite lots of time to make adjustments and to make sure that everything will go well during the final demo as you only have 1 chance if you won't choose to do the early demo (which the deadline is 1 or 2 weeks before the final demo)

sections.content: basic electronics stuffs with some complicated equations such as KCL, KVL and some Arduino programming.
sections.teaching: Extremely good teaching, I am one of those students who never go to lessons in university but Professor Song is the only professor in that semester where I never skipped his classes and even paid full attention during his lectures. I still remembered that he sent an email to us after knowing our grades for midterm were not satisfactory, teaching us that "Life does not have grading, there is no A+ students or C- students", definitely one of the most inspiring professors.
sections.grading: I got B- but still Professor Song has taught me not only a satisfactory ELEC course, but a valuable life lesson.
sections.workload: Its a 4 credit course so it a little bit heavier than usual, but still the content of labs are fun and quite easy to complete, otherwise there is not much work.

sections.content:
A project oriented course. It teaches all the knowledge you need to have in order to build and program an autonomous vehicle and also the theories behind, including basic electronics, PWM, transistors, sensors, KCL&KVL, logics, and arduino programming. The content overall isn't difficult but definitely not easy.

This course consists of lectures, labs, tutorials, group project, lab midterm, written exam and mini contest(optional). The hardware part of the vehicle is built during the labs, while the software part has to be done during free time. The written exam takes place near the end of semester.
sections.teaching:
Prof Song is a good teacher. He explains the concepts clearly and thoroughly with his own notes. He also advises us on major selection and our future.

The tutorials are useless. The tutor introduces the content of the labs only. Go to the labs directly and skip all the tutorials is fine.
sections.grading:
Lab midterm 20%
Written exam 20%
6 Lab assignments 20%
iPRS quiz during lectures 10% (almost all lectures have iprs)
Project demo 25%
Project report 5%

My grade:
Lab midterm 20/20 (similar to past paper given)
Written exam 87/100
6 Lab assignments 20/20 (must hand in during the lab)
iPRS quiz during lectures 10/10 (only best 70% counted)
Project demo 25/25
Project report 5/5

Total: 97.4%, A+

Many students aim at perfection and got very high marks, so you must work hard to get a good grade.
sections.workload:
As this is a 4 credit course, its workload is definitely heavier than normal 3 credit course. Although they don't take attendance, you must attend all labs and almost all lectures to get full mark in quiz and lab assignment. I spent 2-3 days in the lab to finish the project and spent another whole day to write the report.

All in all, the workload is a bit heavy but hard work pays off.

sections.content:
This course teaches the basics of electronics like ohms law and basic circuit analysis. The main part is to build a vehicle that follows a line on the track(instructions and materials are provided). You'll need to code an Arduino MCU to control the logic which is miles easier than pure logic gates.

It is not that far from high school physics: transistors, PWM, truth table, K-Map, logic gates, KCL&KVL.

KCL & KVL are about the only new concept but you can simply use ohms law for more than half of the question in the written exam.
sections.teaching:
Lectures cover the topics as mentioned in the content.

Tutorials are just a recap and usually unnecessary.

Labs account for most of the grades and it is helpful to plan ahead for the next lab. Prepare space on your breadboard for other components and do colour code your wires for debugging purpose.
sections.grading:
Lab midterm: 20%
Written Exam: 20%
Lab assignment: 20% (minimum 4 attendance to attend the final project)
In class iPRS(only counts highest 70%): 10%
Project: 30%
    Project Demo: 24+1% (the 1% belongs to returning the box)
    Report: 5%

There's a mini contest that you can sign up for if you get 20 or above in the demo. It is to repeat the whole thing in the demo, and then back to the starting point. The fastest group with a perfect run guarantee an A grade.

Do mind that this course has become highly competitive and it takes a 90+% for an A. Most are just checklist items tho.
sections.workload: Not much work if you were merely finishing the tasks if you have a clear plan and logic flow of the program, fine-tuning may take some time but it isn't hard.

sections.content: The content is just about right for first year students.. Manageable and fun at the same time
sections.teaching: Teaching is alright, the prof sometimes digress from main content but it helps to make the material less dry
sections.grading: The grading is rather straightforward but bellcurve is rather steep for tests and all.. To receive a good grade, one should aim to constantly achieve jear full marks for all tests
sections.workload: The workload is rather manageable, in fact very little.. no assignments, just have to turn up for lectures, and tests and project

sections.content: Very easy and straightforward. Quite interesting with good practical applications.
sections.teaching: Great teaching
sections.grading: As long as you do well on the midterms and do not mess up the final project, you should get a good grade. There are two midterms, a conceptual midterm, and a practical midterm conducted in the lab. There is no final but there will be a final project which you will work on for the majority of the course. The final project has a final project demo day where you will test your project.
sections.workload: Final project has heavy workload

sections.content: Including hardware and software. This sem we use Arduino instead, so light programming is added into the course
sections.teaching: the prof. is great, but need students to ask meaningful questions.TA are helpful, if you struggle on a problem, ask for help!
sections.grading: Lab exam is easy but important, deserver more time on it.
sections.workload:
a lab a week, the last few labs need more time on it.
Mid-term is quite normal, but some student score very hight, which makes it hard to score high.
But in Lab exam is easy to score full marks if you study before.However many of them don't. Better to spend more time on it.

Be aware of the in-class test, don't miss them.

sections.content:
This course is teaching the basics of building a robot, starting from fundamental knowledge of voltage-current-resistence sort of things in DSE physics and different components that are useful in building a circuit.

No attendance is taken in all lectures, tutorial and labs. However, there will be 2-3 pop-up quizzes after the end of certain lecture that count towards the final grade and do not miss them. You have 1 lab partner in the group for the lab and a worksheet will be assigned for each lab.
Has 2 mid-terms (lab and written) but no final exams (project instead). The project is about building a robot with the provided materials. Starting from this semester though, the robot needs to be programmed by Arduino. Students with programming knowledge in C language may have a slight advantage in this project. There is also a mini-contest for those who passes the final project.
Overall, the course is easy for year 1 students to handle even without prior physics experience.
sections.teaching: He is a good professor, encourage students to ask questions during the lectures and open to questions after lectures as well. Avoid chatting during the lecture though if you don't want to be called out, other things like sleeping is fine though.
sections.grading:
Grading consists of 5 parts, including:
1. Pop-up quizzes (After the end of 2-3 lectures, OPEN-BOOK)
2. Lab Worksheets (1 per lab, bonus mark added to those who hand in within the firs 2 hours of the 3-hour lab)
3. Lab Mid-term (Close-book, SOLO)
4. Written Mid-term (Close-book, though exercises with very similar questions will be provided for revision.)
5. Final Project (including both an actual run of the robot and a written report, has quite a long period for preparation.)
(6.) Mini-contest (Get an A grade instantly with a win, outweighs all the above 5 aspects)

Got an A+ with everything full mark except written mid-term (around 93%).
sections.workload:
Workload varies with your lab partner.
Need some preparation before each lab if you want the 2-hour bonus mark.
Final project period is painful if you got free-rided, especially students without programming experience. With 20-40 hours of time allocated, you should have the robots working fine to get a full mark in the run.

sections.content: 2 open book pop-up quiz (6%), 6 labs (24%), 1 written mid-term (20%), 1 lab mid-term (15%), and final project (35%)
sections.teaching: Both the lectures and the tutorials are quite boring, so self- revision is very important. Tutorials are not necessary to attend as you have the following materials and the following tutorials are just focusing on the labs. No attendance will be scored for tutorials.
sections.grading: The grade is not quite satisfactory. Any missing in the lab mid-term and final project will lead you to a bad grading. Many students got full marks in the final project but as they didn't do well in their written and lab mid-term so finally get C range. C range will be received if you only touch the mean.
sections.workload: As a 4 credit course, the workload is quite high. You need to do the lab for 2 hours a week. For the final project, you need to spend about 2 weeks to make to your robotic car by coding, so workload will be much more if you are not quite familiar with coding. If you want to freeride the lab, you will easily fail the lab mid-term.

reviews.instructor: SIN, Johnny Kin OnTANG, YimengSHEN, Shaojie

sections.content: An awesome introduction course. It involves both hardware and software knowledge, and most importantly, the application of it through guidance. Very suitable for year one students.
sections.teaching: I'd say Yimeng helped us a lot during our lab sections, and especially during the last few labs when we were doing our project demo. Appreciate the efforts of the teaching team of this course a lot-very clearly instructed and help was always readily available.
sections.grading: Generally high gradings, so work to perfection if possible, if you want exceptional grades. Pay attention to your groupmate though. A good groupmate helps a lot and can be very encouraging.
sections.workload: Weekly lab sections, not hard at all-as long as you do slight preparation on them and be on time. The labs were the main workload, as there were no final exam (mid-term only) and homework.

sections.content:
Chap 1: Introduction
Chap 2: Components
Chap 3: Energy
Chap 4: DC Power Source
Chap 5: Pulse Generation
Chap 6: PWM Control
Chap 7: Transistor
Chap 8: H-bridge
Chap 9: Sensors
Chap 10: Logics
Chap 11: K-map

At the beginning of the contents, if you have studied Physics in your high school, it would not be too hard to understand the concept as those are what you have studied before such as Ohm's Law. Even though you haven't learned the other concepts like transistors, H-bridge, K-map or etc, it would not be impossible to get a good grade if you focus on the lectures and the tutorial classes.
sections.teaching: Prof. MURCH is really awesome professor. His explanations are very helpful to understand unfamiliar topics. He also let us to feel free to ask questions not only during the lecture but also after the lecture.
sections.grading:
Exams: 1 Written Midterm (20%) and Lab Midterm (15%), No final exam
Quiz: a few Pop-up In-class quizzes (open book) (6% total)
Labs: 6 Lab Assignments (4% each, 24% total); minimum 4 labs’ attendance to be eligible for final project demo.
Project: Project Demo (25%), Arduino Code Interview (5%), Project Report (5%)
sections.workload: The workload of this course is just reasonable. One of the advantages of this course is that there is no final exam so you would have more time to prepare for the other courses' final exams. In stead of taking final exam, you would do final project. Final project will be done by a group of 2 people. If you studied the topics that are taught through the lectures and spend lots of time on it, I believe that you would get a grade that you are aiming.

sections.content: Lab sessions will be fun if you have a friendly teammate.
sections.teaching: I couldn't really understand what professors were saying since they murmured a lot. Yet, slides were good enough to learn necessary materials.
sections.grading: The mean was quite high for the final project, but it's easy to get in A range.
sections.workload:
Lab sessions usually took 1 - 2 hours. Other than that, did't require much study since all necessary materials were provided on tutorial sessions. Just read over tutorial notes before labs and quizzes.
Final project required some effort, but most of the stuff were already done during lab sessions.

sections.content:
The course basically teaches the basics of electronics.
It teaches about transistors, logic gates, Arduino coding and several types of integrated circuit. It clearly gives us the taste of the electronic engineering. The course is really fun.
sections.teaching: Professor is very helpful and kind. He is very willing to answer all the student's question even after the class hours. He explains in detail and he sometimes give the extra information which is good for us to know.
sections.grading:
Most of the students finishes the project with perfect run. So, the grading almost depends on the midterm lab and lectures, which are quite easy if you understand the lectures fully.

The grading scheme is:

Mid-term exam = 20%
Mid-term lab = 15%
6 lab works = 24%
Pop up quiz = 6%
Final project = 25%
Arduino code interview = 5%
Project report = 5%
sections.workload: There is no homework at all. So, only final few weeks will be quite busy to finish preparing for the final project. Other than that, there will be very little workload.

reviews.instructor: SIN, Johnny Kin OnSHEN, ShaojieTANG, Yimeng

sections.content: No final exams, 2 pop-up quiz, 6 labs, 1 written mid-term and one lab mid-term. 35% marks is obtained by the final project. (25% project demo, 5% interview, 5% report)
sections.teaching: Although the English pronunciation of TANG, Yimeng is not very well. If you know Putonghua, she is a very good professor which can answer all of your difficulties.
sections.grading: The average marks of the course is very high. You need to take higher than 98 marks to obtain a A+ grade. Only a C+/B- can be received if u scored mean in the course total marks.
sections.workload: Quite high

sections.content:
quite easy to understand
introduction to electronic engineering
ELEC1100 is designed to provide the fundamental knowledge on the basic electrical engineering, components design and skills needed for the design, implementation and evaluation of a robot and its subsystems.
It will cover the basic electronic engineering principle and techniques.
Hands-on laboratory sessions, complemented with lectures and tutorials, are provided to allow students to have a systematic view of the electronic engineering principles.
Students will have to apply the knowledge and principles learnt to design and build a functional robot by themselves.
sections.teaching: interesting
sections.grading:
not leng grade as it seemed
85% and u get a B
89% still B+
92% still B+
Exams: 1 Written Midterm (20%) and Lab Midterm (15%), NO final exam
Quiz: a few Pop-up In-class quizzes (open book) (6% total)
Labs: 6 Lab Assignments (4% each, 24% total); minimum 4 labs’ attendance to be eligible for final project demo.
Project: Project Demo (25%), Arduino Code Interview (5%), Project Report (5%)

sections.workload:
have to attend lesson (there are pop-up quizzes during lessons, u can take the quizzes in other lessons)
weekly lab
tutorials (no attendance)
final project (2 people in a group)

sections.content:
Basic physics electronics and some other in-depth stuff. (You can read it from other reviews). They are quite interesting I think but it takes a bit brain juice to understand each and everything taught. Lectures are useful for lab cuz you'll know what you are doing. (it's ok if you don't understand everything but if you mess up anything you'll be in deep trouble and you'll be extremely confused and have no idea what you are doing during the labs.)

***I definitely recommend you to know all the stuff*** cuz it will help you everything in the course.
sections.teaching: Not very intriguing to be honest and progress slightly slow in my opinion but that's ok I think. The English slightly difficult to hear (maybe because it's a bit monotonous...). But very enthusiastic and willing to answer your questions.
sections.grading:
Overall: ~95% --> A

Good grade course ONLY if you are good at computer science OR have a very very logic mindset and you are a person who is very careful about every step.

Midterms:
Lab: 13 out of 15 (mean 10, +1 s.d.); Written: 89/100 (mean 78.2, +1 s.d.)
Get your concept clear and remember the stuff (not much to memorize, to be honest) you will ace through your midterms. Only reasons you will fail: Don't know what is going on throughout the course, or else you will do fine.

Labs:
Full mark for everything, you also should expect this, cuz even you have problems, raise up your hand and ask TA for help, they literally will do it for you (that's my case).

Project:
Do the labs perfectly then you'll have a good start. That's why LABS ARE VERY IMPORTANT. Not many tips for the final project but if you know and like computer science, the task should be easy for you. but there is one thing for sure
***READ IF YOU WANT PERFECT RUN***
1. Build everything carefully and don't try to mess up anything cuz debugging is painful.
2. Complete the program bit by bit, DON'T COMPLETE IT IN 1 GO cuz you'll be likely to fail the whole thing. Start with the first task, then the next, then after that. Gradually build the program while constantly testing your car.
3. If you face a problem, rethink your approach and don't rush through things, you need to get your head clear to find a solution.
sections.workload: Spend lots of time in labs that's for sure. Not many revisions are needed if you already understand everything during lectures. BUT for the final project, I cannot determine how much time you will use, some already have perfect run during the first demo (at least 1 week earlier than the last trial). In my case, some wires are connected incorrectly and I cannot find it so I unplug the whole thing (Yes I know its dumb but I did it) and rebuild everything from lab01 to lab06 within 2 hours and it worked. Unless you mess up big times or you are confident with your logic and concentration and carefulness, don't rebuild the whole thing no matter what. I spend around 8 hours of extra time to finish the thing (exclude lab time)

sections.content:
Introduction course to electrical engineering. This course aims to build a robot car that can follow a white path on a black mat.

Most of the content is covered in high school physics, which is most of the area tested in mid-term. The latter part of the course more focus on the constructing your own robot car, some new ideas like PWM and KMAP will be taught.

Contents include DC power, PWM, transistors, Hbridge, sensors, logic and KMAP.
sections.teaching:
Teaching is ok.
If you know the content, you don't really need to attend the lecture, but there will be open book pop quizzes in lectures. Tutorials only prepare you to do the next lab. TA only read out the powerpoint.
But TA is really helpful in lab and final project.
sections.grading:
A really clear grading scheme.
- 20% Written Midterm
- 15% Lab Midterm
- 6% Open Book Pop-up Quizzes in lectures
- 24% Lab Assignments
- 25% Project Demo
- 5% Arduino Code Review
- 5% Project Report

Lab assignments and project related marks are easy to get full marks.
If you understand the powerpoint slide and what the lab is doing, you can get a full mark in pop-up quizzes and all lab assignments.
If you spend time on the final project, you can get a full mark in the last 35% of marks.
I got 96.2 finally, grade A.
sections.workload:
Not much workload. All lessons will end at the last two weeks of the semester for you to do your project.

But it depends on how is your lab mate. If he/she work helps a lot then the workload is light.
Six labs throughout the whole semester, you must attend at least four of them. But you should not miss one of it since it will largely affect your project demo.

It changed to use Arduino Code to program the car, which is much easier.

sections.content: A broad outline of the hardware part of electronic engineering. Also included some basic programming knowledge of c++ because this term the logic was designed by Arduino. But this course won't cover how the ICs work so you just put them together to maintain certain functions.
sections.teaching: I don't know how other professors develop their lectures. But Johnny's courses were a little boring. I think the most exciting part is the labs. You can really learn something through the labs.
sections.grading:
The grading is good. The midterm is very important because this is almost the only chance for you to get A range.
Exams: 1 written(20%) and lab(15%) mid-term; no final exam
Quiz: a few pop-up in-class quizzes(open book)(6% total)
Labs: 6lab assignments(4% each, 24% total); minimum 4 labs’ attendance to be eligible for a final project demo
Final project (35% total): Project Demo (25%), Arduino Code Interview (5%), Project Report (5%)
Mini-contest: Groups score 20or above on Project Demo are eligible for the contest. The champion group in the mini-contest will be guaranteed to obtain A grade.
sections.workload: The final project cost me a lot of time. But there's almost no other work you need to do.

sections.content:
The content of the course includes elementary knowledge about electricity (simpler than the DSE Physics electromagnetism), simple circuitry-building, basic logics and programming. The lectures are concise and organized, which should be easy to follow.

You will be given plentiful time to finish your tasks in each lab session. Being careful enough, you should be able to complete the assignment fast.

The mid-term examinations only cover the first 3 items. Preparing for the exam should not be too stressful, and scoring high in the written exam should not be difficult.

The final project is about making a line-tracking car in a group of 2. It is quite an interesting activity, but the problem-solving part could be frustrating.
sections.teaching:
The lecture is quite good. Being said the course is easy, parts of the syllabus could still be unfamiliar to some people. Johnny emphasizes a lot more on the important stuff, and will give you a satisfactory answer should you have any questions.

The tutorials can be considered a briefing section for the next lab session. No pop-up quizzes during the tutorials, so attendance is optional.

The TAs are very patient and helpful. They do not mind helping you debug (given you have tried that yourself) and sometimes offer advice that makes your lab session or project easier.
sections.grading:
Written mid-term examination 20%
Lab mid-term examination: 15%
In-class pop-up quizzes: 6%
Lab attendances/assignments: 24%
Final Project: 35% (25% project demo, 5% interview, 5% report)

Overall Score: 92.8/100
Letter Grade: B+

B range is very achievable. However, if you want to fall within A range, you will have to score 95/100 or above in overall. The course focuses on elementary knowledge, making the A range a highly-contested area with narrow cut-off.
sections.workload:
The main sources of workload are lab sessions and the final project. If you have a decent labmate, you should be able to finish them in a reasonable time frame. However, most of the times your labmate would be pulling your legs if not freeriding. Be ready to finish the final project alone and fix the faults committed by the labmates.

For your reference, in my case my labmate almost never showed up during the project period. He also managed to fire a key component multiple times, forcing me to suspend working on the project.

sections.content:
Introduction to fundamental electronics.

The first few lessons are probably for students who didn’t take physics at high school. Basic electromagnetic(AC, DC, V=IR, P=IV) is introduced at first which is high school stuff. Later on, you need to learn the functions and structures of some electronics components such as the resistor, capacitor, ICs(Regulator, inverter, comparator, counter, H-bridge), diode and transistor. PWM control, logic, K-map and sensors are also taught. More advanced topics like sequential logic and programming language are not included in midterm but you need the concepts to help you finish the final project.

Everything is taught step by step and you should be able to catch up without attending the lessons. But there are two/three pop-up quiz.
sections.teaching:
Incredible. The professors and TAs are helpful.

Professor Murch is friendly and willing to answer our questions after the lessons. The lessons are a bit boring because of the contents. However, you can understand the content deeper and clearer by attending the lectures

Dr Tang is responsible for the lab and tutorial sessions. Her ascent could be difficult to understand. But she is very familiar with the circuits and super helpful. She helped my group to solve some challenging technical problems effectively and quickly. Better ask her if you face any crazy problems during the labs.
sections.grading:
Well, the grading is good. B range or even A grade is not difficult to achieve. But you need to be hardworking since many students are getting high marks.

Almost everyone scored full marks on assignments and the final project. Most likely the score of midterm and quiz would decide your grade.

My grade: A(~96-97%)
sections.workload:
You need to find one partner to do 6 labs(3hrs each) and the final project together. Choose wisely! Your workload definitely depends on your partner. You can either choose your partner or wait for random arrangement.

There are 2 lectures, 1 tutorial and 1 lab section every week. Workload increases significantly during the final project period. However, you can finish this course before dealing with other final exams.

sections.content:
ELEC1100 is designed to provide the fundamental knowledge on the basic electrical engineering, components design and skills needed for the design, implementation and evaluation of a robot and its subsystems.
It will cover the basic electronic engineering principle and techniques.
Hands-on laboratory sessions, complemented with lectures and tutorials, are provided to allow students to have a systematic view of the electronic engineering principles.
Students will have to apply the knowledge and principles learnt to design and build a functional robot by themselves.
sections.teaching: Pro Song's class is so good and he is very enthusiastic to reply our questions.
sections.grading:
Grading is so good.
If you got mean in midterm and got full marks in the final project and all labs, then should got A range.
sections.workload:
Exams: 1 Written Midterm (20%) and Lab Midterm (15%), NO final exam
Quiz: a few Pop-up In-class quizzes (open book) (8% total)
Labs: 7 Lab Assignments (22% total, first 6 labs 3% each, final lab 4%); minimum 4 labs’ attendance to be eligible for final project demo.
Project: Project Demo (25%), Post-demo Interview (5%), Project Report (5%)

sections.content: The content mainly focus on logic gates and simple circuit design. The concepts are easy and basic.
sections.teaching: 9am class is difficult to focus however the lectures notes are self-explanatorily and easy to follow.
sections.grading: The grading is good as long as you make the final project works.
sections.workload: There are pop-up quizzes during lectures, a lab test and a final project. Quizzes are easy as long as you read the lecture notes beforehand. Lab test is basically the same as the lab sessions however, a good de-bugging skill is needed. The final project is most challenging and time consuming.

sections.content:
Although it is an introductory course for electronic engineering, the stuff they teach is a little bit daunting for students who have not studied physics in high school, mostly when they introduce electronic circuits and logic gates.

-Energy & Power
- DC Sources
- Pulse Generation
- PWM Control
- Transistor & Diode
- H-bridge
- Sensors
- Logics
- K-map
- Sequential Logics
- Programming Language, Part (I): Variables

sections.workload: The workload greatly depends on your labmate, as you have to finish building an electric car to get a full mark on the project demo. If you have a good labmate to carry you, the workload of this course is very light. However, if your labmate relies on you the entire time, then congratulations, good luck.

sections.content:
Mainly about the electrical components, such as diodes, transistors etc. Most of the lectures and labs are helping you to build the car.
However, programming is needed to control the car, but not much is taught (only 3 lectures), most of the students with no knowledge of programming still don't know how to program the car. Self study is recommended...

Final project is to build a robot that could trace the line and avoid going to the wrong branches. Knowledge about state machine is recommended but it was not taught during the course.
There are 3 demo sections, 1 early demo and 2 final demos. I recommend taking the early demo as you can usually finish the car very early and the early demo give you 4 trials instead of 2 trials in the final demo.
There is also a mini-contest which could guarantee you an A if you got the first place. However, doing a round-trip is much harder than 1-way trip, you would need much more time tuning for that. Also, I saw some failed in the mini-contest due to various reasons... So better not rely on that to get an A. (only half of the ~40 registered teams went to the contest as most of them can't do it, and only 8 managed to do a perfect run.)
sections.teaching: There are pop-up quizzes during some lectures, so it is recommended to attend the lectures.
sections.grading:
The grading is fair. Full mark for labs, final project, lab midterm, 8/10 and 10/10 for quizzes, 93/100 for written midterm and got A+.

AFAIK most of the students got full marks in labs and final project. So, midterm and quizzes are really important for the grade.
They are easy, so you would need a really high mark for a good grade.
sections.workload:
The workload is low through out the course. Before the final project period, there is basically nothing to do, what you need to do is go to the labs. For the project period, you can basically manage to finish the car in 5 hours, so the workload is not high.
However, for the final project, please remember to check you car about 2 hours before your demo, probably it won't work when you check it and you need to fix it...
It is better to follow the suggested breadboard connection, so you could quickly figure out which wire is lost when you debug. Also, be careful in tuning the sensors, too sensitive would bring you harm during debugging...

sections.content:
LECTURES & TUTORIALS
- Please refer to "TEACHING".

LABS:
Mandatory, six in total. 2 people working in a group. Find a friend to work together, else you will be matched with one.
The labs are easy. TAs are helpful as well. You shouldn't have any problem to get full mark here. Spending a little time reading through the lab notes beforehand is rather useful.

MIDTERMS:
There are lab midterm and written midterm.

Lab midterm:
You should learn how to use things like DSO and signal generator properly. Also remember not to mix up normal diode and Zener diode.

Written midterm:
Not quite difficult. You should get good results if you study well. Pay more attention to the parts about PNP and NPN, as well as the connection of ICs. Those questions are slightly harder.

PROJECT: (guide attached below)
Have to be done near the end of the semester. Your group (same as that of lab) have to construct an autonomous vehicle to move along the white line with curves and splits. You really have to spend some time on it, like testing Arduino codes. Around 4 to 5 days in lab is enough.  Enjoy the art of debugging your vehicle!

Demo, interview and report required for the project. Take the early demo if you can finish the car early.

Early Demo: testing x2, trial x4
Normal Demo: testing x1, trial x2

MINI-CONTEST:
Optional. Complete a round-trip of the project map as quick as possible. Winning group members will be guaranteed getting an A. My line sensors are not working well in a contest so I didn't get any prize. There will be prizes for top 10 groups, ranging from trophies to society paper. The fastest group finished in 39 seconds (round-trip), whereas 35 seconds is the time limit of getting full mark for project demo (one-way). Pretty hard to win the contest. Don't try to rely on the contest to get A. But if you can do so, you can simply ignore everything else.
sections.teaching:
The choice of instructor does not matter a lot. I don't really pay attention to what he said in class. His accents are a little bit weird but still able get what he is saying. He just simply read those powerpoints with slightly more explanations, which is rather mundane. Reading notes yourself is enough to get a good grade.

LECTURES:
There will be pop-up quizzes in lectures. Attendance of lectures is encouraged. Content-wise: For the first few weeks, those are only DSE Physics basic stuff, like dealing with circuits and resistors. Pretty easy. Don't really have to listen if you have DSE physics background. For the next few weeks, something new is taught, but pretty easy to understand. I think reading lecture notes by yourself is okay as well.

Topics mainly include:
  Energy, power source,
  pulse generation, PWM control,
  transistors, H-bridge, sensors,
  logics, K-map, sequential logics,
  Arduino & programming language

TUTORIALS:
They are not important. I almost skipped all.
sections.grading:
Quite Good.

Labs: 24% (@4%)    [20/20 for all labs]
Pop-up quizzes: 6%   [10/10 , 9/10 respectively]
Lab midterm: 15%   [14/15]; mean = 10.7
Written midterm: 20%  [84/100]; mean = 80.2
Final project: 35% [35/35]
  **the final project includes:
   (a) 25 marks demo
   (b) 5 marks interview after demo
   (c) 5 marks report
No final exam.
My final grade: 95.5% => A

p.s. I heard that someone got 93.x in total but finally got B+. Probably the grading scale is kind of narrow. Make sure you get high marks from every lab and quiz. A little can matter a lot.
sections.workload:
Before the project period:
Very low. Just don't forget to attend the lecture and labs. Nothing else have to do.

Project period (mid to late Nov):
Medium. You really have to spend some time to work on the car. Staying at the lab for 4-5 days, and 3-4 hours per day is pretty much enough. Having a responsible lab-mate is kind of important. However, I still see some groups that have to stay in the lab overnight.

sections.content: The aim of the course is for your group (groups of 2) to design a robot car that can follow a white track by itself. First part of the course teaches the concepts behind the robot car, such as electricity, PWM signals used to control the motor speed and logic (NOT, AND, OR etc.). Second part of the course briefly introduces programming with the Arduino Nano to implement logic on your robot car. After learning all this you are expected to build on the concepts used

sections.grading:
- 1 written exam (20%)

- A few pop-up in-class quizzes (open book) (6% total)
- 1 lab midterm (15%)
○ Week 8-9, during regular labs
- 6 labs (4% each, 24% total) — minimum 4 labs attendance

○ Project demo (25%)
○ Arduino code interview (5%)
○ Project report (5%)
There is no final exam, only midterms. This means that only content taught before the midterms will be tested, which is very good. There may be one or two quizzes after the midterm but those are open book so that is not really a problem.

There is also a contest for those that achieve a good score in the final project demo. The winners of that contest are guaranteed an A.

sections.content:
Starts off with basic electronic physics like current, voltage. (If you took physics dses, the first part should be pretty smooth). Then it moves on to more complicated electronic components like H-Bridges, Transistors, etc.

The main objective of the course is to make a functional car using electronic junk to move in a given circuit.

They don't take attendance in lectures, but they do in labs. The course is highly focused on practical work, so you can skip lectures and read online notes. Lab attendance is more important.

BUT, they have quizzes in lectures that aren't announced. (3 quizzes in total, from my experience) It's good to be well informed about them by people in your own lecture or in other lectures. If you skipped a lecture that had a quiz, you could go to the next lecture available in the week to take it.

ZERO Tutorials attended. lol.
sections.grading:
Grading is fair, but not generous. (I don't know the exact percentages, refer to other reviews, soz :p)

This course has labs, a midterm and a project, BUT NO EXAM. (yay?)

Labs take up a moderate chunk of the percentage, but if you go to them regularly and know what youre doing, it's gonna be easy. You can always ask STAs / TAs for help during lab. If you finish early, you get bonus marks to your lab. Make sure you print out the labs before going to the room. (there are printers on the way to the lab, so you can print right before then) [I attended every lab, and got good marks in every one. I got the time bonus in the beginning of the course, but didnt in the ones later cuz the content got harder]

Midterms also take up a large amount of the percentage, there is lab and written mids.

DO NOT UNDERESTIMATE THE DIFFICULTY OF WRITTEN MIDTERMS. Many people's grades got screwed over cuz of midterms. If you want to survive midterms, there is a pastpaper example in canvas' files. The sample is very similar to the midterms, so try to go through that and absorb it with every fiber of your soul. The other tutorial notes are kinda good too. [I got pretty good marks in midterms thanks to the sample paper]

LAB MIDTERMS ARE PRETTY STRAIGHT FORWARD. It's very similar to the labs you'll do, just remember how all the components and equipment in the lab work and you should be ok. Bring a calculator (cuz i forgot mine) and pen/ pencil.

The Project is a nightmare if you dont know what youre doing, and it takes up a lot of your grading. (More elaborated in WORKLOAD)

Got an A- overall
sections.workload:
The workload isnt that much in the beginning, just labs (and maybe some pop quizzes) and done, but it will become a hella lot harder later on cuz the content becomes a bit harder and mainly cuz of the PROJECT.

Tips for the project
- Get a good teammate to work with for labs, cuz lab partners are gonna be your project teammate (preferably a friend). If they're lazy/ dont know what theyre doing, you're gonna die (unless you can carry the team like a mule, TEAMWORK IS NEEDED). Collaborating with your partner doesnt always mean you both need to meet up at the same time slot. You both can work on it in the lab whenever you can. just make sure you know your roles.

- Try team up and communicate with other groups (The grading is absolute, so no bell curves like the dses. Multi group collaboration is beneficial for everyone.)

- Be organized (If your entire breadboard is messed up with random components, debugging will be hard. Once your labs are done, you can clear it up for the project)

- Check your components if they work and on how they work ( If the circuit is not working, you're not always wrong, some sections of the bread board dont work + some of the sensors are faulty)

- Keep on testing your electro-car and try finish early. (If you go for the earlier final demo, youll have 4 attempts to run the car in case any errors occur. going for the later one only gives you 2 attempts, which is bad. Have timeslots to work on your car whenever the lab is open)

- Understand the way the components work. (You can always google image the components and see what pins do what. Not doing so might cause your components to short circuit and could even break your breadboard)

- There are going to be some allnighters, guaranteed. So prep some caffeine up for it.

- AFTER THE PROJECT, YOU WILL BE INTERVIEWED ON HOW YOUR CAR WORKS. Make sure you know how the components work to make the car run as it does.

-glhf

get full marks in (quizzes, lab midterm, lab+bonus, demo, interview and report...) except written midterm 98/100. End up 99%+ and get A+

sections.content:
ELEC1100 is designed to provide the fundamental knowledge on the basic electrical engineering, components design and skills
needed for the design, implementation and evaluation of a robot and its subsystems.
It will cover the basic electronic engineering principle and techniques.
Hands-on laboratory sessions, complemented with lectures and tutorials, are provided to allow students to have a systematic view
of the electronic engineering principles.
Students will have to apply the knowledge and principles learnt to design and build a functional robot by themselves.

Before mid-term, simple to moderate calculation, so concepts on physical like resistance, current and voltage and semi-conduction are required
Well, things got quite abstract after the mid-term.
sections.teaching:
SONG was like a father, he was keen on sharing his care and vision on university education. inspiring lectures.

BUT, as for the tutorials. Damn the ta's accent is way to heavy. I barely heard anything. It was difficult to focus.

ANDDD ultimately i would prefer spending my time on learning arduino than ICs circuit, although admittedly this course is a foundation of the path of any electronic knowledge.
sections.grading:
For whom only care abt the grade of their final project, should focus on k-maps construction, function and implementation of ICs(includes those did't mention in class, e.g. multiplexer) and how to use DFF. Done! Better self-learn then follow the class after mid-term, especially the working principle of ICs, it was kind of waste of time to figure out what was going on regarding earning a good grade.

While written mid-term was comparably require less effort then the final project. Just get used to the questions by studying the examples in every ppt and past paper.

For lab midterm, be aware of the usage of multi-meter along side with circuit construction(particularly resistor network construction). Pretty depends on luck, like final demo.

Quite good grade.
The most useful part of this review:
3 in-class quizzes: 6.9333% ((10+6+10)/30) (mean:7.1+6.1+7.7)
Lab: 22%(pls strive to get full marks in this section)

lab midterm: 11% (11/15)(mean:8.3/15)
demo: 14% (mean: 19.1/25)

report:5%

Grading is so damn good despite of my failure in my demo.

You see, we screwed up in the demo. Yet, frankly, we spent 2 overnights along side with countless day time hours to fix the problem on y-splits. Because we knew nothing abt dff, we basically f*cked.
You paid but not necessarily gain.
START the final project as soon as possible. The lab always welcomes you.

sections.content:
1. Basic Electronic Components
2. Power Consumption and Delivery System
3. AC Power Sources and Rectifiers
4. DC Power Sources and Regulation
5. IC and Pulse Generation
6. PWM Motor Control
7. Transistor and Diode Circuits
8. Motor Control by Transistor and H-bridge
9. Kirchhoff’s Laws
10. Sensor
11. Binary Number and Logic Gates
12. Boolean Algebra and K-Map
13. K-Map and Adders
14. Multi-bit Adder and Comparator
15. Sequential Logics and RS Flip Flop
16. Timing Diagram and D-Flip Flop
17. Finite State Machine

The content is very interesting, basic, and useful in electronic engineering field.
Originally, it's very easy, and then gradually, the content is getting harder. However, it's very satisfactory to make sense of all the materials with a larger scope after finishing the whole semester.
p.s. I usually understand the concepts taught in lectures after finishing the weekly tutorial and lab.
sections.teaching:
The Professor's teaching is great! He always encourages us to raise questions, creating an aggressive learning atmosphere. With this atmosphere, it helps student understand the content efficiently, and it sometimes introduces us creative ideas.
Besides, the professor is  always patient with your questions. He is willing to teach you with various methods, in order to let you understand.
In short, Professor Ross is indeed a nice teacher!

sections.content:
Introduction to electronic engineering. The course introduces different electronic components like diode and transistors, and some knowledge about logics used in electronics (Binary, flip-flop etc.). Although they don't require you to know everything in detail, sometimes things are not easy to understand.

Components and circuit structures introduced would be used to build an electro-robot (an electronic car). The car needs to go through a given track by itself (using given components and your design of the circuit). They provide you all the materials you need.
sections.teaching:
Prof. FAN is passionate in his teaching. He is a professor from Mainland China but his English is easy to understand. He is also willing to answer your questions. He would try to know whether the students understand the contents.

The female TA (I forget her name...) is worse. She can't explain things clearly. I tried to focus on her teaching but I just couldn't understand. It's hard to explain but she is not as good as Prof. FAN in explaining the ideas.

In labs you may seek help from TAs if you have questions. They are quite helpful. When something doesn't work and you have no idea why, they are usually willing to spend time helping you to find out.
sections.grading:
I have forgotten the break-down percentages of the final grade. Please try to look for it in other reviews if you wish to know.

Things in written mid-term was quite hard to me (maybe I'm just bad T.T) . I got like 30-40%. In the lab mid-term I got slightly above mean.

Since I have a good groupmate and we both were willing to work on the project, we got full mark in everything in the final project.

Got B grade finally. It's not that harsh actually.
sections.workload:
It is a 4-credit course, so the workload is surely heavier than 3-credit courses, but not that terrible indeed once you have got used to labs.

One lab mid-term, one written mid-term, no final exam but a final project. No homework.

There are lectures, tutorials and lab sessions every week. A few sudden quizzes in lectures.
One lab per week. You need to form a group with one groupmate for all the lab work (can't be changed later). The tutorials introduce things you need to know for the coming lab (some of them actually overlap with things talked about in lectures).

Before mid-term, labs are experiments that let you get your hands on the components introduced and learn how to use the equipment.
After the mid-term exams, the circuit built in labs is for your final project (the car), and you keep progressing it in every lab.

A final written report needs to be submitted after the final project demo.

This course is a fun and unforgettable experience for me. Instead of just sitting in lectures, you really have a chance to build a robot from group-up and utilize the components you have learned about. Of course it would be quite painful if your groupmate is a free-rider. Better have a friend to study this course with you (REMEMBER: You two need to be in the same lab session).

sections.content:
The course content is all about basic electronic knowledge. The first few weeks are things in the high school physics, and the content become more technical such as logic and memory chip after midterm.
It is actually an enjoyable course to learn basic knowledge and apply them into a visible project.
sections.teaching:
Murch, Ross is really passionate in teaching. He always encourage us to raise questions during the lecture, and try his best to clarify the concepts.
The TA,  Tang, Yiming, helps us a lot in the lab. Despite the poor accent, she is kind and nice to answer any question about the lab.
sections.grading: The grading is pretty good. Take care of the written and lab midterm, and put some time on the final project, A+ can be earned easily. There are some pop up quiz in lecture but doesn't count a lot to the final grade. ~
sections.workload: The only workload is the final project. A little bit tricky but spending 1~2 nights is basically enough. You can even pay for a design. Just keep an eye on your battery, which makes an enormous different during your demo session.

sections.content:
In ELEC 1100, the final goal for every student is to design and build a car with given materials that can follow the white lines in the map and do different but right behavior under some rules when at the cross.
In the lecture, professor will give detailed explanations about the working functions behind the car step by step. Students are not required to fully understand the theory behind the functions while they need to be sure to know the logic in the function system and apply the functions well.
In the tutorial, TA will go through the lectures and do the groundwork for the coming lab, such as giving some examples of possible bugs.
In the lab, students need to follow the instructions to fulfill the tasks.

Speaking of the policy, there's no attendance requirement. However, concerning the pop-up quiz, absence may lead to the loss in grading.

What impressed me most is the uncertainty in the project. Unexpected bugs occur frequently, some will even show up at the demo stage, leading to a severe failure in demo. The consequence is a severe failure in grading.
sections.workload:

But note that in the final two weeks, many students will spend over 20 hrs to deal with the projects, some will even work overnight. But it really depends. I saw group spend less than 10 hrs to finish the job as everything went smoothly.

sections.content:
Like physics,  Then it'll start to get a little more in depth, talking about: transistors, KCL&KVL, PWM, truth map, K-Map and logic.Content builds on high school physics, and gives a neat introduction into concepts in electronics; in my opinion it is useful even if you are not required to take it. On top of all of these, this course is more practical-based, as Prof. Song put it: "Here, labs are more important than lectures; don't skip labs even if you skip lectures."

The Project Period in the latter part of the course gives you the freedom to design your very own logic to instruct a robotic car to complete a route (e.g. staying on track, choosing the correct branch to go, bouncing off at goal). For me it is the part of the course "you can learn most" because you are doing everything on your own. The lab opens 24h except when having labs for other courses, and the teaching team would help you with everything you need including consulting about your design. It requires textbook concepts, practical skills, debugging skills, teamwork, creativity; if not trains them.
sections.teaching: Prof. Song explained things super clearly and interestingly.
sections.grading: Good Grade!
sections.workload:
Lectures are short (50 mins) and not mandatory, Prof. Song had hand-written notes all scanned online, plus powerpoint slides uploaded frequently to Canvas. To be frank you can skip lectures and manage your own time to cram materials, though not much needed to cram anyways. Tutorials are similar, but they are more directly useful in terms of helping you to complete the lab work efficiently. Midterms are not particularly difficult in terms of content, you need to be calm and revise to the point of understanding is enough, no need to do much exercise, but be sure you are familiar with the lab machines as you rely on them in the lab midterm.

Labs and Project
- How much you can score in labs and project depend largely on your use of time. There were quite some instances where students get frustrated when they cannot finish the labs on time for the bonus or even before the lab session ends, for me it was the lab midterm; and getting desperate when they find out not much time is left for the Demo to come. It is unwise to lose scores because of this, so all I can say is be careful
- Your time invested is proportional to your performance. (Some say you would sleep in the lab in the project period...)
- Raise questions when you encounter problems, so the best way is to be attentive enough to be able to raise questions.

sections.content:
Content builds on high school physics, and gives a neat introduction into concepts in electronics; in my opinion it is useful even if you are not required to take it. On top of all of these, this course is more practical-based, as Prof. Song put it: "Here, labs are more important than lectures; don't skip labs even if you skip lectures."

The Project Period in the latter part of the course gives you the freedom to design your very own logic to instruct a robotic car to complete a route (e.g. staying on track, choosing the correct branch to go, bouncing off at goal). For me it is the part of the course "you can learn most" because you are doing everything on your own. The lab opens 24h except when having labs for other courses, and the teaching team would help you with everything you need including consulting about your design. It requires textbook concepts, practical skills, debugging skills, teamwork, creativity; if not trains them.

Lectures/Tutorials/Labs:
- Energy, Power
- Basic components [lab: basic equipment]
- AC sources [lab], DC Regulation [lab]
- Pulse generation, PWM control [lab]
- Transistor [lab] & Diode & H-bridge
- KVL, KCL -------- Written & Lab midterms up to here
- Sensor [lab]
- Logic [lab], K-map, Adders
- Combinational logic, Sequential logic, D-Flip Flop
- Finite State Machine
* Tutorial prepares you for lab work with a practical insight into the lecture textbook knowledge, each lab has a tutorial beforehand

Partnering:
Starting from lab 3 all the way to lab 7 and the whole project, you will partner with someone and work in a group of 2.
You can choose your own partner and declare that together on Canvas.
If you do not yet have one by the start of lab 3, you will be matched with one.

For fun:
Mini-Content
- This is not required by the course but you can win prizes (from USB memory sticks to a quadcopter)
- This time you need to do a U-turn and complete the track from start to end then from end back to start.
- Criteria:
    1. Distance
    2. Speed
    3. Elegancy: tidiness of the car appearance (breadboard)
    4. Simplicity: no. of logic gates used to achieve the effect
- For high aimers: don't bother to demolish everything and start over. We didn't do that and costed us a rather complex design in the end.
sections.teaching:
Prof. Song explained things super clearly and interestingly.
His approach to lecture is to write on the whiteboard (speedily), and he keeps everything simple and write as he speaks. He stresses on the point that being an engineer we are practical, so for example when doing some math he would skip the steps as long as everyone knows what's happening. Sometimes he uses the powerpoint for a slide or two but you can still see things link together. A very good presenter.

Before the start of lecture he usually plays some videos about recent robotics advancements, leaving behind inspiring remarks to let us imagine and think.

He makes jokes and tries his best to interact with his students too. Most of the students become friends with him. He would poke you to start a casual conversation. After lecture, he welcomes questions and we pretty much flocked to his room. Cantonese/Mandarin/English all okay. He tries to understand your level of understanding towards the concept and then interprets the concept from your perspective.

The last lecture was memorable. It was no longer about the course but more about coaching about university life and career, owing to the enrolment situation that most students here are freshmen. I can see that Prof. Song wanted to do more than transferring knowledge, but to make sense out of going to university as a norm, hence educate us to exploit our university life well.

TAs are nice also. Yimeng might have some issues with her English accents but she was kind and willing/passionate about teaching. Others assist lab operations as well as project period support well.

The teaching team was and probably will be generous enough to offer you support and even tell you not to worry in every possible ways. So just do your best, and have fun building!
sections.grading:
1. Exams: 35%

- Lab Midterm:15%
- There is no Final exams

2. Quizzes: 8%
Open book, no exact number of times, but having 3 is normal
For me the third quiz took place after midterms, so it was pretty much the only assessment on textbook knowledge after the midterms
Used to replace counting attendance in a way, as is usually conducted at the end of lecture time (enough to call your missing friends to come maybe)

3. Labs: 22%
- Lab 1-6: each 3%
- Lab 7 (final lab): 4%
- Bonus: each 3% if you and your partner can finish the lab in 2 hours
   (out of 2h50m), but only count towards this 22% (even if you have extra bonus points they would not count towards other breakdown parts like midterms)
* Attend a minimum of 4 labs to be eligible for Project Demo

4. Final Project: 35%
- Project Demo: 25%
     -> Separates into Early Demo or Final Demo which you as a group can sign up for. Early Demo would be around one week earlier but offers more chances for trials plus more time to demo. Recommended if your group can make it as you can lower risk of having sudden faults
    -> Safe measure is to videotape a run for backup. I heard that there must be some devastating malfunctions happening each semester which would ruin a few groups, sometimes it is the hardware problem and not even your design fault. You can get half (12.5%) maximum if you decide to use the video instead of demonstrating in extreme cases.
    -> Breakdown scores available for partial completion of various extents, so a perfect run can give you a full 25%
- Post Demo Interview: 5%
    (Conducted right after the demo, simple questions will be asked and both members of the group will have to answer. The purpose is to punish free-riders if found so if you understand what you have been working on, you are good to go)
- Project Report: 5%
    (Requires to mark contribution of each member, a 50%/50% would mean there's no free riders. The report should not exceed 6 pages, and to be handed in after the demo as the very last part of the course; instructions will be given but format is free)

You and your partner score the same in most of the labs and project breakdowns.

sections.content:
The course starts with very basic physics stuff, V=IR, W=VI, etc.
Then the contents advance to more electrical field, transistors, resistors, capacitors, timers, pulse-width modulation (PWM), KCL and KVL are contents covered before the midterm.
After midterm, logic gates, boolean algebra and flip flops, finite state machines are also introduced.
sections.teaching: Song is a very nice professor. He teaches with heart, and is willing to answer any questions (course relavent or irrelevant, both OK). He uses handwritten notes for the class instead of PPTs.
sections.grading:
It has been said that course has a very good grade because lots of people get a good grade in this course (B+, A-, A, etc.)
8% - Pop quizzes in class
22% - Lab sessions
25% - Final Demo
5% - Final Demo Interview
5% - Report
20% - Written Midterm
15% - Lab Midterm
Every coin has its two sides.
Because the contents are easy, the midterm thus have a very high mean for both the lab and midterm.
the mean for written midterm is around 70/100, because most contents were easy. mean for lab midterm was around 9.5/15.
Because there are so many students with good marks, if you fail to review some parts of the lecture notes or you screwed up the midterm due to some reason, you will easily get below mean for midterm.
REMEMBER TO REVIEW KCL AND KVL!!!!!!!!!
You may also encounter stupid mistakes such as forgetting to turn on DC during lab midterm, which costs lots of marks.
The final demo really depends on luck. My car was able to have a perfect run before the demo 9 out of 10 times. But somehow my car cannot turn at the Y splits and oscillates there, which caused my demo to be a complete disaster. It was too dependent on luck.
I got an extremely bad grade at the end. Minor mistakes and random luck could cost a lot in this course as lots of them could outperfom you.
My review might be biased, but it is exactly what I experienced in the course.
sections.workload:
Before midterm, the workload is not too much. Just review on the important parts and you should be OK.
After the midterms, the main source of workload come from the project that you will do.
You are required to do a car. Details are covered in other reviews.
But however, the results are not always satisfactory, and it is too dependent on luck.

sections.content:
Building an electro-robot, with Navdroid and ICs.
Basics of electronics and EM are taught.
Topics:
Energy (AC/DC Power Source)
Pulse Generation/Pulse Wave Moderation (PWM)
Transistor
Kirchhoff's Voltage/Current Law

After the mid-term, the topics are related to the final car.
Logics/K-map
Sequential Logic
Flip Flops

sections.teaching:
Selected Prof. Shen's lecture. The lecture is a bit boring, yet essential to know what you are going to do in the final project. You can email/contact them if they want a chat about the car, or any ideas/obstacles that you think of. Prof. Song visits the lab periodically and you can ask questions meanwhile.

Dr. Tang is the IA of the course. She is responsible for the demos and lab sessions throughout the course. You can find her for administrative matters and such.
sections.grading:
You have no problem in getting A range if you successfully build a working car that can fulfill the requirements in the demo. You can choose whether to join the early demo that you have more time to fine tune (to be exact, 2hrs). You only have 15 mins(?) to finish the 2 trials with no return in the final demo. You can join either one, but NOT both.

Exams:
Written Midterm (20%)
Lab Midterm (15%)
No Final

Quiz: a few Pop-up In-class quizzes (open book) (8% total)

Labs: 7 Lab Assignments (22% total, first 6 labs 3% each, final lab 4%); minimum 4 labs’ attendance to be eligible for final project demo.

Project: Project Demo (25%), Post-demo Interview (5%), Project Report (5%)

You can easily get the whole project part if you did not freeride your partner (Please, don't do it in this course, the workload is HEAVY)

Get full marks for most labs, missed one quiz, mean for both mid-terms, full mark in project, overall: A.
sections.workload:
Mediocre/Heavy (C-):
Labs and PROJECT PERIOD (Majority of workload is in late semester)

The lecture materials are not hard to understand. If you have any questions, you can ask the Profs. The main part of the workload lies in later part of the semester, when you get hands-on experience in building the car. You get access to lab and make the car from scratch. A part of the car is already done in the 7 labs (The things you need to think and design are the directional/turning/speed settings, which build the brain of the car)

sections.content: The content is quite useful in your preparation for the elec major. sections.grading:

There are also 7 lab sessions throughout semester that is about 10% of your grade.

sections.content:
Through hands-on labs and term project, complemented with lectures
and tutorials, you will be able to:
Analyze and design simple analog circuits, combinatorial and sequential logic circuits, and design and implement simple feedback control strategies.
Build and debug real engineering system following a hierarchical design principle.
Work in a team environment: learn and practice effective project and time management.
Execute a complete project from problem formulation.
Problem with conventional teaching:
Current education system was developed in the industrial revolution and does not evolve to the information era
Teaching knowledge, but not how to apply the knowledge
School never tells students that the taught knowledge may become obsolete upon graduation design/implementation, up to verification and documentation.

sections.content:
Basic electronics.

The course consists of 20 lectures, 10 tutorials, and 7 labs. It talked about high-school physics, diodes, transistors, PWM control, KCL & KVL before midterm, and sensor, logic gate, K-map, logic design after midterm. The content is not very difficult, but you can go deeper if you are interested.

I think the amount and level of the content are quite appropriate for an introductory course.  However, most of the content are not necessary for the final project.
sections.teaching:
Fine.
Clear notes are released before class. In fact, you don't need to go to lecture and tutorial with the notes.
Instructor and tutor are quite helpful.
Fan is from mainland and we can ask questions in Putonghua:)
sections.grading:
Fair grading.

22% Labs (7 times)
8% Pop quizzes (3 or 4 times)
20% Written midterm
15% Lab midterm
27% Project
3% Interview
5% Report

It's easy to get full marks in labs and in-class quizzes. Many of my friends also got full marks in written midterm, but I think the calculation was a little difficult.
Lab exam was challenging. Many didn't have enough time to finish all three questions. You need to be very familiar with diodes, resistors, wire connection, and the equipment.
The project required much effort but it's not so hard to achieve perfect run as long as you have prepared for it.

Getting A+ with 96% overall. My friend gets A with 92% overall mark.
sections.workload:
Not that heavy for a four-credit course.

No assignment, but it's better to go through the guidance before labs.

Workload became bigger during the project period. My teammate and I each spent about 15 hours in the lab. The report cost us 10 hours. It's a good idea to start early.
